en: The Third Chapter, "The Retention of Immeasurable Qualities," from the Commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* composed by Ācārya Haribhadra.

Since the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is to be explained immediately after the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), and because the disciples are inclined toward the fruit due to the fact that there is little more to be said [regarding the former] and they tend toward the result, [the author], speaking primarily of the activity of the Path of Cultivation of ultimate purity which is about to be described, says: "He who this," and so forth.

In this Perfection of Wisdom, which is the very nature of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the Lords—the Bodhisattvas such as Mañjughoṣa and others—dwell through the yoga of identity with the intention of protecting the world. Whoever shall grasp this [Perfection of Wisdom], both in its literal text and in its meaning, through knowledge consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, and shall master it at all times—for such a person, because the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) is not destroyed, the attachment to existence is poison.

Because its nature is burning, passion (*rāga*) is fire; because its nature is affliction, hatred (*dveṣa*) is a weapon; and because delusion (*moha*) causes harm through its coldness, it is water. It does not "cross over" [the path] because it is utterly destroyed by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and thus it does not manifest. According to the principle of obstruction, it should be understood that even external things such as poison do not cross over—that is, they have no power—[in the presence of this realization].

In this very way, Māra and even his retinue—the faction of Māra—find no opportunity, fault, or vulnerability through which they might seize [the practitioner] and cause him harm; such is the meaning. Following the discussion of activity (*kāritra*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) must now be explained. That path is twofold, distinguished by being with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*). Among these, the one with-outflows is threefold, characterized by mental attention (*manaskāra*) consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and rejoicing (*anumodanā*). The one without-outflows, moreover, is twofold, having the nature of purposeful application (*abhinihāra*) and ultimate purity (*atyantaviśuddhi*).

Therefore, first of all, by means of attention consisting of resolute belief (*adhimukti-manaskāra*), one accumulates merit even from phenomena that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). Just as a lump of gold [is distinguished] from base metals, this [resolute belief], although its own nature is not yet fully perfected and it generally takes as its object the wholesome phenomena seen through resolute belief, must be described as being—by virtue of encompassing all goals and primarily regarding the sphere of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—the cause for the accumulation of great merit when engaged in activities such as writing [the scriptures].

Furthermore, that [resolute belief] is categorized as being for one's own benefit, for the benefit of both self and others, or for the benefit of others, depending on whether the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for the conceit "I" has been abandoned or not.

To speak of the conviction regarding one's own welfare, he says: "Of the one who has attained final nirvāṇa," and so forth. For the sake of benefiting those beings to be trained through nirvāṇa, there may be some single being who [sees] the Tathāgata—who has manifested nirvāṇa by means of an emanation body—as possessing the seven precious substances:
musāragalva, vaidūrya, silver, crystal, gold, along with red pearls, and emerald as the seventh.

One causes a stūpa, a shrine made of the seven precious gems, to be built and worships it; in this manner, one should connect the meaning as follows: one causes stūpas made of those seven precious gems, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges, to be built for the Sugata, until thousands of millions of world-systems are completely filled with such stūpas, and likewise worships them.

In this manner, even if as many beings as there are—conceived as being infinite millions—were to construct that many stūpas and all of them were to perform worship with celestial flowers and other offerings throughout the kalpas of the three periods of time, and furthermore, were to continue performing worship even after that subsequent period; [the merit would still not equal that of one who hears this Dharma].

And whatever other person, having generated resolute faith for the sake of accomplishing their own welfare, writes down this Mother of the Sugatas in the form of a book—consisting of these very texts—and upholds it by retaining both the words and the meaning through the application of the powers of knowing what is possible and impossible, and so forth; and honors her with flowers and other offerings, [attains the same result]. This refers to the Blessed Ones, the Guides, from whose presence [the teachings] have arisen, and who perform various kinds of benefit through the possession of the ten powers.

Having thus indicated the different categories of merit, he says "kala" and so forth, concluding the subject at hand: whatever mass of merit is acquired by performing worship at the aforementioned stūpa, that does not equal even a fraction—a remote part—of the merit of the one who performs the worship while traveling. Therefore, it is said that for one who desires their own welfare, faith (adhimukti) should be generated toward the Perfection of Wisdom alone. (2–4)

Immediately following this, explaining the conviction in the welfare of oneself and others through the equality of self and other, he says: "The Great Knowledge," and so forth. Because all those Lords of the World (*lokanātha*) who have passed away in the ten directions because their teaching has ceased, those who are yet to come because their teaching has not been attained, and those who are currently present because their teaching is being destroyed—all of them, having trained in this knowledge (*vidyā*), have become and will become unsurpassed leaders of physicians (*vaidyanāyaka*), due to their teaching the means for pacifying all obscurations along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*) in an unerring manner.

Therefore, this Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*), the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), is connected with the Blessed Ones. It is "pacifying" (*śamanī*) because it removes suffering—such as physical pain consisting of bodily unpleasant sensations—as well as distress such as verbal distraction through mental exertion, and grief such as mental despondency arising from separation from desired objects; and it is so called because it brings about the attainment of Buddhahood for the entire world, for the whole mass of sentient beings, without exception. // 5 //

If it is argued that [this mantra] brings about benefit only through the arising of the Tathāgatas and not through those such as the Bodhisattvas, he says: "And those who... and so forth. Those Bodhisattvas who, being intent on the welfare of sentient beings and possessing compassion, always practice the conduct of giving and so forth—they too, having trained in this vidyā and become wise, will attain enlightenment.

Whatever conditioned pleasures belong to the gods and others, and whatever unconditioned pleasures belong to the śrāvakas—all those pleasures should be understood as having been produced from this mother; therefore, it may be said that she is the one who brings about their welfare as well. // 6 //

But how can even a single [cause] produce manifold effects? To this he says: "The seeds," and so forth. Seeds such as those of the *harītakī* and others, when scattered upon the earth, remain because they have not perished through processes such as putrefaction; they arise in succession. Furthermore, according to the principles of *vṛkṣāyurveda*, having obtained a collection of auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*), they yield fruits of various forms. Just as there is a distinction [in the fruit] due to the difference in auxiliary causes, so too is the thought: the Mother of the Victor, though she is one, produces manifold effects such as the state of a Tathāgata.

If it is asked, "Since loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] are also causes for Buddhahood and so forth, why is it stated that the Mother alone is the cause? he says: "As many as... and so on. In general, however many qualities of enlightenment (*bodhiguṇa*) there may be, such as loving-kindness and the rest, which are cultivated as being conducive to awakening; and in particular, the five perfections (*pāramitā*), beginning with generosity (*dāna*), which exist as dharmas—[all these are contained within her].

Since all those are the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are non-erroneous precisely because of the non-apprehension of agent, object, and action; this means that she alone is the primary cause. // 7 //
But why does this [attainment] not arise as a follower of those? He says: "By that very [means], etc.

Having personally conquered the various types of vehicles, strife, and weapons, those belonging to the Wheel-turning Kings (cakravartin) consist of gold, silver, copper, and iron, respectively, in descending order.
Those who possess one, two, three, or four continents.

According to this statement, just as any one of the four types of universal monarchs (cakravartin) proceeds by whatever path he travels, so too—due to the sovereign power of that merit—the seven jewels beginning with the wheel-jewel and the military host consisting of the assembly of elephants and so forth follow that very same path; likewise, in its non-erroneous form, this perfection of wisdom, which is the realization of the selflessness of the world by the Victors, arises in the mental continuum of a yogin by way of that very same path.

Because all qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the rest are produced through its sovereignty, they are "Dharmas" by virtue of maintaining a non-erroneous form. They arise correctly and directly because the realization of all Dharmas is preceded by non-perverted knowledge; therefore, [the Mother] does not arise as a follower of anything else. Thus, it is said that one who desires the welfare of oneself and others in every way should generate resolute faith (*adhimukti*) toward her as a mother. // 8 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the third chapter, titled "The Veneration of the Stūpa of Amitāyus, the Possessor of Immeasurable Qualities and Retentions."

The fourth chapter, "The Proclamation of Qualities. Immediately following this, in order to speak of the resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) for the welfare of others—based on the fact that the nature of the world has been taken into one's own self—the text says, beginning with "Śakra": "O Kauśika, of these two portions thus established, which portion would you take? Thus questioned by the Jina, he asks the question: [43a] "If all the relics of the Jina were to fill every part of the earth, and if Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā were to be gathered into a single heap (*cūḍikābaddha*) by being piled up to the very top of their crests, this would constitute one portion."
The meaning of the verse is that he spoke thus: "At that time, I would take up this very portion of the Prajñāpāramitā."

To the question, "What is the reason for this lack of respect toward the Tathāgata? he says, "For what reason? In response, he says, "No," and so forth: "It is not that I lack respect for the bodies of the Tathāgatas; rather, just as a man who has taken refuge with a king receives honor everywhere in the territories conquered by him solely through the king's majesty."

Likewise, the Buddha, relying upon the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), is the element (dhātu) that serves as the cause of the noble qualities; through its sovereignty, he receives worship everywhere throughout the three realms. Therefore, because those relics have been thoroughly permeated by the perfection of wisdom and are endowed with its majesty due to being completely suffused by it in every way, living beings worship them. Thus, may I take hold of the perfection of wisdom. 2.

If one were to argue that there can be no worship once the Blessed One has entered final nirvāṇa because there is no longer a physical basis for it, the author speaks by way of an analogy, beginning with the words "Just as a jewel," etc. Just as a precious gem is endowed with all excellent qualities because it drives away non-humans and other such beings, and is therefore obtained as being beyond price due to its exceeding value; and the casket in which it is placed becomes worthy of veneration through the power of the jewel—so too is it here.

When this [jewel] is extracted from that casket, all those [qualities] become composed of virtues because they have that very jewel as their cause. In the same way, such are the qualities of this supreme perfection of wisdom, because even when the Blessed One has entered parinirvāṇa, by the sovereign power of the Mother, the relics of the Victor (jinadhātu)—which possess the characteristics described in the *Dhātuparīkṣāsūtra*—become the cause for the mental clarity of fortunate beings through the performance of miracles, and thus receive worship.

Therefore, one who desires to embrace the qualities of the Victor through resolute conviction in the welfare of others should grasp this Perfection of Wisdom by applying oneself to writing it and so forth; because it pacifies all calamities, it is liberation—that is to say, Nirvāṇa. By this, there would be the attainment of resolute conviction in the welfare of others. (3–4)

[Objection: But why is it that, although one is devoted to the other perfections such as giving (*dāna*) and so forth, a threefold devotion is taught primarily only for the Mother of the Victors (*jinajanani*)? [Response: He says, "The precursor," and so on. Because, through the non-apprehension of agent, object, and action, wisdom (*prajñā*) becomes the precursor when giving is being practiced, since it is what first initiates the activity; and likewise in ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), vigor (*vīrya*), and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This is because the previously mentioned word [“precursor”] has a different connection [in each case].

It is both a grasper and a producer of apprehension; because it brings about the full nourishment of wholesome dharmas such as generosity and so forth, it must be applied toward their non-dissipation, their non-deviation into the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and others, and their long-term endurance. For this purpose, that single [wisdom], when practiced even in brief due to its being pregnant with compassion, reveals all dharmas—beginning with the production of the thought of awakening—as if they were directly perceived.

The meaning is that it is precisely here (or rather, in that context) that the threefold resolute belief (*adhimukti*) is taught; or else, the resolute belief that exists in the *Prajñāpāramitā* is itself [the same] everywhere because there is no distinction. // 5 //

He states this by way of an illustration, beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*) and so forth: Just as in Jambūdvīpa there are many thousands of millions of trees, which, due to the diversity of cause and effect in their respective orders, become of various kinds and manifold, and possess many forms because of the distinctness of their own natures.

There can be neither plurality nor distinctness among them, because they are designated by different words; nor is there any specific differentiation, because their nature consists solely in the exclusion of non-shadow. At most, they receive and attain the numerical designation and expression "shadow-body" (*chāyākāya*). This is said when the essential nature of the body is being described or indicated—that is, when it is pointed out. Likewise, through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), by means of the purification of the three spheres (*trimandalaviśuddhi*) and the creation of a different state free from error, they come to exist as that which has been transformed (*pariṇāmita*). // 6 //

These five factors, beginning with generosity, are the perfections (*pāramitā*) of the Victors; when all these [virtues] such as generosity are dedicated by means of the mental application of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*) to be described later regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and Buddhahood, they become perfections.

Because of the connection with the preceding phrase "of the Jinas," the five perfections beginning with generosity (*dāna*) are thus [established] in two ways; wisdom (*prajñā*), however, is secondary, yet it is well-known as a perfection because it accords with the primary purpose. Thus, all six perfections, within the primary Perfection of Wisdom, proceed toward and attain a single method and a single nature, due to the exclusion of non-perfections and the exclusion of [incomplete] perfections, and because they lack various distinct forms by being denotable by the term "perfection."

That is to say, because it illuminates the reality of the non-erroneous nature of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), whatever resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) one has toward the Mother [Prajñāpāramitā] through writing and so forth—namely, the purification of one's intention—that very same [conviction] should be established as existing everywhere; thus it is stated. (7)
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the fourth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of Qualities."

Having understood that this threefold resolute belief (*adhimukti*) must be practiced by being free from the defects of counterfeits (*prativarṇaka*), [the author] speaks first by way of logical sequence (*anvayamukhena*) for the sake of abandoning those counterfeits, beginning with the words "If he... and so forth. "If he" refers to the Bodhisattva who regards imagined form (*kalpita-rūpa*) up to mind (*citta*) as impermanent due to their non-existence; and he regards the conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*) form and so forth as impermanent because they do not persist beyond a single moment according to the principle of cessation (*āvṛtti*).

However, having resolved through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of the grasped and the grasper and so forth, he proclaims it as impermanent. He proceeds by means of a counterfeit, disregarding the intended meaning; not understanding the true nature of things, he sometimes brings about destruction and establishes [false views] regarding the restraints (*yama*). The sense is that this occurs because there is no existence of anything possessing different characteristics (*vidharmin*).

He also speaks by way of negation, beginning with "In which," and so forth: In that resolute conviction regarding the reality of things, one does not perceive form, nor even sensation; rather, through non-arising in accordance with reality, one knows all phenomena to be of the nature of emptiness. This is that wisdom which is the practice of the supreme perfection, a correct resolute conviction free from any counterfeit—this is the meaning. // 2 //

Immediately following this, in order to inspire the bodhisattva who cultivates the threefold resolute belief toward further progress by rejoicing in their truly existent qualities, the Buddhas and others perform praise (*stuti*), laudation (*stobha*), and eulogy (*praśaṃsā*) in due order; thus, to speak of this praise and so forth, he says "as many as... and so on: Suppose someone were to establish all sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of as many Ganges rivers as there are Buddha-fields, in the state of Arhatship.

And whoever, having written this Perfection of Wisdom consisting of syllables with any kind of resolute faith, should give the book to other beings, would produce a merit more distinguished than that. // 3 //

"What is the reason, what is the cause for the giver of a mere book to possess superior merit compared to one who performs distinguished acts of worship? In response, he says: "Those here," and so forth. Having heard this verse of the *Prajñāpāramitā* from a source that is both distinct and connected, the Śrāvakas quickly attain their own liberation, the Pratyekabuddhas their own awakening, and the Tathāgatas the awakening of a Buddha, through reflection and meditation.

In this regard, those who here take up the book of your mother are trained and are the best of speakers, for they cannot be overcome by the proponents of false doctrines. Because they understand all phenomena as being signless within emptiness here in the three types of enlightenment, therefore, the gift of the three types of enlightenment through the provision of a complete cause is the reason why the giver of the mere book possesses greater merit.

Since this is an illustration, it should be understood that whatever aspiration (adhimukti) Bodhisattvas have toward their mothers is also caused by exceptionally distinguished merit. Because its essence is the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), the Bodhisattva alone is the basis of all phenomena, and nothing else. (4)

Therefore, he says "of that which is non-existent," and so forth, to show that one is encouraged by praise and the like through emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Just as in the world there is no production of a tree if its material cause—the sprout—is absent, how could there be the arising of Śakra and the others whose existence depends upon it? Likewise, without the *bodhicitta* as the material cause, there is no arising of the Victors (*jina*) in the world; how much less, then, could there be the manifestation of Śakra and the others, whose activity consists in attending upon and meditating on the Tathāgatas? // 5 //

If it is argued that this is unestablished because beings are set toward Buddhahood and so forth even without the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), he says: "Like the sun," and so on. Just as when the solar orb emits a thousand rays of light, beings exert themselves in their duties through the correct comprehension of objects resulting from the departure of darkness.

Likewise, because the bodhicitta—which has emptiness and compassion as its essence—arises from the thorough knowledge of the true nature of the world, it is born for one who always knows the world. By means of that knowledge, through the power of uplifting the world submerged in the ocean of suffering by awakening to the reality of phenomena (dharmatattva), they practice in the qualities of Buddhahood and so forth, which are a hundredfold [superior]. The intention is that otherwise, one who lacks compassion and lacks skillful means would not engage in the pursuit of Buddhahood and the like. // 6 //

Having demonstrated through the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that all phenomena are dependent upon the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), he speaks by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—preceded by an example—to show that in its absence they too would not exist, beginning with the words "Just as... and so forth: "Just as, if the serpent-king were not present in the Anavatapta lake, from where could the flow of the Ganges River arise here in Jambūdvīpa? It would certainly not exist. Consequently, in the absence of those rivers, fruits and flowers would not come into being due to the lack of nourishment from their water."

Furthermore, the jewels of the oceans do not come to possess their manifold forms merely through contact with the breaking of the water; likewise, in this teaching, if the bodhicitta—which has emptiness and compassion as its core and pertains to the Tathāgatas—did not exist, then the stream of knowledge that arises from its power, which effects the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful, would not exist at all even in this entire world.

Consequently, in the absence of gnosis, there is no perfection of generosity and the other perfections; there is no increase in the qualities of the perfections, nor is there enlightenment—which is like the ocean—consisting in the fulfillment of one's own welfare because it cannot be easily attained. Nor are there the qualities that arise subsequent to Buddhahood, which constitute the fulfillment of the welfare of others. (7–8)

Having thus explained the greatness in detail, he concludes by saying "as many as," and so forth: however many lights there may be anywhere in the world—whether the stars such as Jupiter and others, fireflies and the like, or even living beings—all of them circulate with their radiance for the purpose of illuminating the universe. And when even a single ray of light released from the solar disc should exist, then all the aforementioned hosts of stars and so forth would possess no luster whatsoever, not even enough for a mere flickering appearance.

In the same way, the assemblies of śrāvakas and others do not equal even a fraction [of the merit of the bodhisattvas]. Therefore, it should be understood that praise and other honors are bestowed upon the bodhisattvas by the Buddhas and others. // 9 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Enumeration of Merit."
The sixth chapter, "On Rejoicing and Dedication.

Now, following the mental application of resolute belief—which has been praised, lauded, and extolled by all the Buddhas—the mental application of rejoicing (*anumodanā-manaskāra*) must be explained, as it is to be practiced through rejoicing. Furthermore, that [rejoicing] is of two kinds because it is preceded by dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). For instance, when one dedicates one's own roots of merit and then rejoices for the sake of nourishing the subsequent mind, that is the first kind. But when one rejoices in giving and so forth performed by others for the sake of restraining minds such as stinginess, that would be the second kind.
Therefore, in order to explain the second mental application of rejoicing (*anumodanā-manaskāra*) by way of its predominance, he says:

"As many as... and so forth. Whatever merits consisting of giving, morality, and cultivation are produced by the hosts of Śrāvakas—if a Bodhisattva rejoices in them, this being an illustration that includes those bound [to the world] and others as well—[FŏŏTNŏTĕ:[48b] although there is a variegated painting on the leaf, yet the leaf itself is not perceived].

One who thinks, "I dedicate," is attached because one has reached a state of all forms of clinging through the perception of action, agent, and activity. Therefore, because it is contradicted by valid cognition and is of the nature of a misconception, that which is being perceived cannot be truly dedicated. // 5 //

If that is so, how then is there dedication? To this he says: "And that," and so forth. If a bodhisattva knows that these dedicating factors have ceased through their inherent destruction and are exhausted through the destruction of accumulation, and knows that very factor to be exhausted, yet understands that in Buddhahood there is no mental formation (*saṃskāra*) of dedicating a factor—that is, a basis of meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*)—then, because it is like the dedication of an illusory person, by him it becomes truly dedicated. // 6 //

Thus, when the agent, the object, and so forth are understood through the non-apprehension of all phenomena, for what purpose then is apprehension said to exist in some instances? He says, "And that," and so on. If a bodhisattva, even while realizing the illusory nature [of things], should grasp at an extreme view—thinking, "This alone is the truth; everything else is delusion"—then he does not perform dedication at all, because apprehension is of the nature of perversion (*viparyāsa*).

Now, if one does not form an attachment even to the signless (*animitta*), it becomes "dedicated" (*pariṇāmita*) because it is correctly directed toward awakening (*bodhi*). For just as food that is poorly prepared is said to be "exquisite" to a small degree because it produces pleasure in its taste despite resulting in suffering at the end, so too the perception of the dedication of pure qualities (*śukladharma*) and so forth—though a cause for falling away from awakening—is described by the Blessed One as "exquisite" to a small degree because it produces clarity of mind in beginners.
Therefore, the point is that one should not form an attachment to that [perception]. // 7 //

This entire principle stated regarding the mental application of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-manaskāra*) should also be understood in the case of the mental application of rejoicing (*anumodanā-manaskāra*). For this very reason, having explained these two types of mental application in detail, he concludes by saying: "Therefore, one should rejoice," and so forth. Since there is a fault in apprehending [phenomena] in any manner whatsoever, therefore—even without the realization that things are like an illusion—by way of necessity, just as those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, [rejoiced] because their merit depends on causes that are delightful only when not analyzed; [so should one rejoice].

Whatever kind [of merit] they recognize—its source being the production of effects that cannot withstand analysis, its characteristic being the absence of a nature that is either one or many—in that way I rejoice, and in that way I dedicate it; thus one should train in rejoicing and dedication. For even in this way, because there is no error, there is right practice; such is the opinion. //8//

If it is asked, "What benefit would there be from that? he says: "And in this way," and so forth. In this very manner, through the yoga of non-attachment, one who perceives merit as being made of leaves—since awakening (*bodhi*) is its defining characteristic—rejoices; yet, because his engagement is not erroneous and he does not perceive a [separate] fruit, he does not reject what is bound. Therefore, by virtue of speaking words of rejoicing and so forth in the manner described, he becomes one who speaks as the Victors have spoken, due to his utterances of rejoicing and the rest.

Furthermore, by virtue of his acquisition of a vast abundance of merit, he surpasses all those bodhisattvas in the world who still perceive [objects as real]; for, transforming [merit] and rejoicing according to the principle already explained, he is a bodhisattva who is brave and fearless due to the absence of any fear of perceiving [phenomena]. This is the meaning.

And in order to indicate that the sequence of these two types of mental attention is not fixed, [the author] first explained the mental attention of dedication in the *Śatasāhasrikā* and subsequently explained the mental attention of rejoicing; however, it should be understood that here the order is otherwise. // 9 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the sixth chapter, titled "Rejoicing and Dedication."
The Seventh Chapter: On Hell.

Immediately following the threefold impure path of cultivation (*sāsrava-bhāvanāmārga*), the pure path of cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanāmārga*) is to be cultivated. Since that [pure path] is twofold according to the distinction between cause and fruit, he says "those born blind," and so forth, in order to first explain the path of cultivation characterized by actualization (*abhinirhāra*). Just as millions of beings born blind—lacking a charioteer and thus having no guide—are unskilled because they do not know the nature of the path, how could they be wise regarding entry into the city? Indeed, they are not at all.

Likewise, without wisdom characterized by actualization, these five perfections—generosity and so forth—are devoid of vision; being like those born blind, they lack eyes. Because they lack a guide to enter the stages such as the Joyous (*pramuditā*) which constitute the path leading to Buddhahood, they are without a leader and are unable to reach the Great City of the Knowledge of All Aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), that is to say, they cannot attain awakening through direct contact. // 1 //

Where, then, is the attainment of these eyes? He says: "In which," and so forth. When, in the interval—that is, in the middle—between the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), which are characterized by ultimate purity, there should be wisdom (*prajñā*) grasped through giving and the other perfections by the power of cultivating the state of the cause of the untainted (*anāsrava*); at that very moment, because of the attainment of the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*), which is the cause of all excellence, the eye becomes truly attained. For this very reason, from the attainment of Buddhahood, giving and the rest receive the designation of "perfections" (*pāramitā*).

Otherwise, if one lacks eyes—just as a painter who has mastered his craft might otherwise complete a painting in every way, yet being deprived of sight by the loss of his eyes, fails to produce it and thus does not obtain the merit, its price, or the means for its completion because he lacks the eyes—the thought arises that, in the same way, there would be an absence of all success. // 2 //

If the state of being perfections (*pāramitā*) for generosity and the other virtues arises through the power of the wisdom of accomplishment (*abhinirhāra-prajñā*), from what does that [wisdom] itself arise? To this he says: "When phenomena," and so forth. When one does not perceive—even down to the slightest atom—by means of the wisdom consisting of accomplishment, phenomena such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and others which are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) associated with the Śrāvakas and others, as things to be abandoned; and when one likewise does not perceive even the slightest portion of the white [virtuous] side.

Then, through the realization of its illusory nature, the Bodhisattva’s wisdom itself attains the designation and the name of a "perfection" (pāramitā). What has come into being in the world? It is that wherein not even a mere space remains established in any absolute form; therein, by those born as pure Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—this is the meaning. // 3 //

He states that even regarding the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), attachment is a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*): "If he thinks," and so forth. If he thinks, "I practice in the wisdom of the Victors," which has the nature of such an accomplishment; and if he thinks, "I shall liberate many beings"—the term "many" being used as an illustration—those who are afflicted by the manifold sufferings of birth and so on, numbering in the millions.

Then, because he has engaged in a perverted manner, this bodhisattva is not a "conceptualizer" (*parikalpaka*) regarding the notion of a sentient being (*sattvasaṃjñā*). Furthermore, since the word "not" (*na ca*) is connected with what follows, it means that this is not the practice or realization of the course of conduct of that supreme perfection of wisdom which has been described. // 4 //

Immediately thereafter, the second path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), characterized by ultimate purity, is to be cultivated through the sequential adoption and abandonment of the causes for its arising and non-arising. First, demonstrating the cause for its arising, he says: "He who [attains] enlightenment," and so forth.

The Bodhisattva who has practiced the perfection of wisdom here with direct intent, preceded by the propitiation of the Tathāgatas and other such acts, having been a practitioner through his previous conduct, now possesses no doubt or hesitation regarding the Mother of the Victors due to the power of his realization of the true nature of reality (*dharmatattva*). Furthermore, through the power of his erudition, immediately upon hearing it, he will regard her here as the Teacher; thus, by the presence of the cause for its arising, he attains the path of cultivation characterized by purification.
He will swiftly realize awakening through the comprehension of the reality of all phenomena, and [attain] peace through the pacification of all calamities. // 5 //

Explaining that which has non-arising as its cause immediately after the cause of arising, he says "with reverence," and so forth. Having honored [the Buddhas] through the offering of retinues and the like during his previous course of conduct (*pūrvacaryā*), and having practiced the *prajñāpāramitā*—if not now [he fails]. Due to attachment to the aggregates (*skandha*), association with bad friends, being under the influence of pride (*māna*), and lack of faith in the Mother of the Victors (*jinamātṛ*), because he lacks protection on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) which is characterized by the power of non-arising, he should be understood as being "without protection" (*atrāṇa*).

And having heard it thus, whoever—due to a deficiency in the realization of the profound Dharma and being of small intelligence—shall reject this mother, he, having rejected it, will go to the Avīci great hell. This is to be understood as follows: because of the very rejection of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there is an absence of anyone to uphold the Jewel of the Buddha and the others, and thus one becomes one who has no protector. // 6 //

Summing it up, he says: "To him," and so forth. Since there is thus a fault in lack of faith, therefore you Bodhisattvas should have faith in this Perfection of Wisdom, the mother of the Victors, if you wish to touch and realize the supreme Buddha-knowledge. Just as that merchant, through skill in his own interest, having gone to the island of jewels, does not return from the very source after cutting off [the connection] at the root.

In the same way, having reached the jewel-island of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), the roots of virtue previously acquired proceed without interruption toward further increase; such is the intended meaning. // 7 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the seventh chapter, titled "Hell."
The Eighth Chapter: On Purity.

Having thus explained the cause of realization and non-realization regarding the objects of attainment and avoidance, [the author] speaks first in general terms of the purity of the path of cultivation characterized by ultimate purity, saying: "The purity of form should be understood as the purity of the fruit. This refers to the intrinsic nature of form, such as the five aggregates and so forth.

The purity consisting in the resemblance to an illusion is to be understood as arising from the first fruit (*phala*) and so forth, due to the departure of the clinging to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīya*) regarding the cause; for otherwise, the emergence of the effect that is purity would be impossible. Likewise, it should be supplied that "the purity of the fruit is to be understood from the purity of form," and so on. Having thus stated the general purity of the effect because it is produced by the cause, he speaks of it specifically: "They say that the purity of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) arises from the purity of the form of the fruit."

When the path of cultivation—ranging from the stage of the *anāgamya* up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)—arises in each respective stage through the repeated taking as its object the general principle that "all phenomena are selfless," in order to abandon the nine grades of afflictions such as the "intense-intense" and so forth by means of the sequence starting with the "weak-weak," one attains mastery everywhere through the purification of the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*).

Then, because of the purification of the two states [of the path and the fruit] which constitute the fruit, through the attainment of the path of cultivation characterized by ultimate purity, the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) itself is the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) due to their commonality with the three types of omniscience; thus the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have spoken of its purification. Likewise, it should also be understood that they have spoken of the purification of the fruit-form from the purification of the knowledge of all things.

Because it is prescribed in that manner in the *Śatasāhasrikā*, one might object: "In that case, there is a misconception due to the differentiation of purity. To this he replies: "And omniscience," and so forth. This conventional discourse regarding the differentiation of purity is stated from the perspective of the conventionality of yogins; otherwise, it would be impossible to demonstrate the realization [of reality] through conventionality.

From the perspective of correct reasoning (*nyāya*), however, the purity of omniscience, the purity of the fruit, and the purity of form are undifferentiated due to their equality and emptiness—just like the element of space—because there is no distinction in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Because there is no cutting off of their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) is said to be "uncut. Thus it has been said: "The acts of darkening [the world] and so forth, as well as the paths of the Disciples and the Pratyekabuddhas, and the path of vision with its great benefits, are possessed of qualities pertaining to both this life and the next."
Function, resolute conviction, and being praised, extolled, and lauded;
the two unsurpassed mental attentions regarding dedication and rejoicing.
"Accomplishment and ultimate purity—this is the path of cultivation for wise Bodhisattvas; thus is the Knowledge of the Path proclaimed. (1)

(Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.8–10) Since the thorough knowledge of the path cannot be correctly attained without the thorough knowledge of all things, [the author] says "the three realms," and so forth, in order to explain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Because they have seen saṃsāra and the rest as they truly are through wisdom, the Bodhisattvas have rightly transcended the three realms—characterized by desire, form, and formlessness. Furthermore, because they are dependent upon performing the welfare of sentient beings out of compassion, and because they have removed their own self-nature from the afflictions by attaining mastery, they are "those who have removed the afflictions" (*kleśāpanīta*) while remaining in the world.

By manifesting birth through the appropriation of a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), they demonstrate it for the sake of favoring those beings who are to be disciplined by means of impermanence; yet, because they have abandoned the karma conducive to that [birth] and are free from old age, sickness, and death, they speak of destruction preceded by old age and the like. The thought is that the wise ones are unshakable by the distractions of signs (*nimitta*) when they course in the *prajñāpāramitā*, because they have attained proximity to it through the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) in every respect.

Thus, when the sons of the Conquerors have drawn near, it should be understood that through skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), they do not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa due to their non-perverted perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). By contrast, in the section on omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), it is shown through the negative formulation (*vyatireka*) that because of a lack of skill in means, the Śrāvakas and others remain as they are in saṃsāra and nirvāṇa respectively—due to their distance from the correct perfection of wisdom by virtue of merely attaining their own [limited] realization, and because of their deficiency in compassion and wisdom, through the apprehension of things as real entities and non-entities. // 2 //

Therefore, he says "and in desire," etc., because that which is the antidote for the Śrāvakas and others is the adverse side (*vipakṣa*) for the Bodhisattvas. "In desire" (*kāme*) means in that which is desired; it refers to what is longed for by the Śrāvakas and others as being endowed with aspects such as impermanence. Since "form" (*rūpa*) here generally denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [the verse refers to] one who—whether in form (intrinsic nature), in the world, or in the world of sentient beings and their environment—is attached and clinging to this personage of the Bodhisattva and so forth, due to ill-spoken words, as if stuck in a mire, a place of attachment.

From whatever point it collapses—that wheel of saṃsāra consisting of the six destinies—it revolves because the cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*) have not been abandoned. Because its movement is unstable, it is like a wind-wheel; and because it has never been produced, it is illusory in nature within this world that takes the form of phenomena (*dharma*) and their substrates (*dharmi*). Just as a deer falls into a snare, one must not engage with that [wheel], for it stands in opposition to liberation; such is the intended meaning.

How, then, is this the antidote for the Sons of the Conquerors? He says: "Like space," and so forth. Just as swans and other birds roam in space, yet do not depend upon it because space, being a non-entity, lacks substantial reality; in the same way, Bodhisattvas whose wisdom is awakened roam among form and the other aggregates like birds in space. They do not depend upon them in the form of either the attribute (*dharma*) or the substratum (*dharmin*), because form and the rest lack substantial reality. Therefore, the meaning is that non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) alone is the antidote, since it is free from fault. // 3 //

Regarding the sequence for the cultivation (*vibhāvanā*) of the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted concerning those two opposing factors, he says "He who thinks 'I am form,' etc. in order to explain the equality of the application (*prayogasamatā*). Among the five aggregates, such as form, the Bodhisattva who practices with complete purity through the power of awakening to equality does not engage at the commencement of cultivation because of the absence of attachment (*abhiniveśa*). In this way, through the gradual practice of emptiness, he completely abandons [the opposing factors].

Because he has attained the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), he has completely dried up all adverse factors (*vipakṣa*). Being liberated from all attachments to those muds, he moves within the wisdom of the Sugatas. However, since the Śrāvakas and others move by grasping at form and so forth as impermanent and so on, this [verse] may be stated by way of contrast (*vyatireka*). // 4 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the eighth chapter, "Purity."

The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is to be cultivated through a practice manifested by means of equanimity; for that purpose, he says "in this way," and so forth. Thus, practicing according to the sequence of application, the wise and learned bodhisattva, by negating both the adverse factors and their remedies—such as [the notions that] form and so forth are either permanent or impermanent—cultivates them in the aspect of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

When the path of seeing is attained, through the removal of the bonds of the afflictions that were to be abandoned therein, one goes forth—severed from attachment and liberated—by means of the successive attainment of higher realizations, remaining unattached in the world. Therefore, like the sun released from the eclipse of Rāhu, he shines resplendently; and just as a fire, once applied, consumes a forest of grass, stalks, and wood, so too does he, when applied to cultivation, consume the multitude of afflictions that were to be abandoned therein—this is the remainder [of the sense].

However, it would be implied by the sense that the Śrāvakas and others cultivate their own path of vision through aspects such as impermanence, [following the negation of aspects such as permanence]. Thus has omniscience been explained. And so it has been said:
"By wisdom there is no abiding in existence; by compassion there is no staying in peace. Through lack of skillful means there is distance; through skillful means there is no distance."
"The path of seeing of the Śrāvakas and others is held to be omniscience (sarvajñatā) insofar as it consists of the discordant factors and their antidotes, the application, and its equality. // 1 //

(Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.11–12) Having thus realized the three types of omniscience, for the sake of mastery, one again attends to that very [omniscience] by means of the path of distinction; this is the "complete awakening to all aspects. To explain its characteristics, he says "by nature," and so forth. Because they are like an illusion through cultivation, one sees—that is, realizes—these perfectly pure phenomena as being by nature, that is, by their own essence, the perfection of wisdom, which has the nature of complete awakening to all aspects.

Since the bodhisattva does not perceive an imagined self as a seer, nor does he find any phenomena—such as form and so forth—as established by those of his own school, because they do not exist; therefore, through the realization of the two modes of selflessness regarding persons and phenomena, and by the attainment of all aspects, this is the practice and application of the supreme perfection of wisdom, because it consists in the aforementioned clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Thus it is said. // 2 //
The ninth chapter, on Praise, in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*.
The tenth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Qualities of Retention.

The aspects (ākāras) are to be cultivated through distinguished applications (prayoga). Since these cannot be explained without one who applies them, the author, pointing out the practitioner, says: "Śakra [questioned] the Jina," and so forth. Śakra, while moving among the hosts of gods, questioned the Jina: "How does a bodhisattva primarily apply himself to the practice of the Perfection of Wisdom, which consists of these aspects? This is the question.

The Blessed One said: "One who does not indeed apply themselves even to the slightest degree through the yoga of apprehension toward the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, nor toward phenomena such as impermanence and so forth—because they proceed without error—they are fit to be called a bodhisattva. (1)

To avoid [this objection], he says: "Having practiced for a long time," and so forth. It should be understood that one who has engaged in the practice of this Mahāyāna for a long period of time is intended. A being who has performed service by constructing monasteries and other works for many millions of buddhas, having heard these teachings on the Mother, does not doubt at all that these phenomena—form and the rest—are like illusions, because they are produced through their own causes in the manner of an illusion. Furthermore, he applies himself to training; the meaning is that there is no longer any such thing as a deviation from the way things truly proceed. // 2 //

Now, because it is impossible to explain otherwise the applications (*prayoga*) in the *Jinajananī* [Prajñāpāramitā] belonging to those who act as Śrāvakas and so forth—which are by nature both non-distinct and distinct mental orientations—he first speaks by means of an illustration, beginning with "In a wilderness" (*kāntāra*), in order to demonstrate the overcoming of obstructive factors (*antarāyadharma*) through hearing and so forth.

Just as when a man who has been traveling for many *yojanas* on a road beset by a multitude of calamities sees, through the power of another effort directed toward him, the abundance of cattle-pens or the excellence of forests, he then attains confidence due to the absence of fear from the wilderness; nor does he have any dread of thieves, because he perceives these signs of villages and towns nearby, such as the cowherds and so forth.

In the very same way, when a bodhisattva—who seeks awakening by practicing the dharmas for its attainment—obtains the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) upon hearing it, he attains consolation through the acquisition of the right path. Furthermore, he has no fear of falling into another vehicle, because through the perfection of yoga consisting of hearing and so forth regarding the Mother, he does not attain the stage of an Arhat nor the stage of a Pratyekabuddha. (3–4)

Now, since it must also be explained by describing the activity of bestowing all perfections upon the Mother through hearing and so forth, he says "A man indeed," etc., demonstrating that [bestowal] preceded by an illustration by way of describing the activity of bestowing the Dharma-body: "In the same way, if some man traveling toward the ocean water were to see trees on every side while looking at it, then he should understand that even now the great ocean is still far away."

Then, when one no longer sees signs such as trees and the like, because of being free from doubt, one should become free from uncertainty, thinking: "The great ocean is near; it is not very far away. In this very way, one who has set out for the supreme enlightenment with the intention of reaching it should be understood [as being near]. By hearing this, by reflecting upon it for the sake of its comprehension, and by cultivating this perfection of wisdom of the Victors, [one draws near].

Although he was not personally prophesied by the Leader, the Blessed One, for unexcelled enlightenment, nevertheless, through the power of his application in hearing [the Dharma] and so forth, he will before long attain the enlightenment of a Buddha—the full awakening to the Dharmakāya; such is the meaning. (5–6)

He also speaks by way of demonstrating the activity of offering the *saṃbhogakāya*, beginning with "In the beautiful springtime," and so forth, and "Just as when," and so forth. Just as when a beautiful spring season has arrived, a tree with withered leaves and withered branches does not long before it properly brings forth leaves, fruits, and flowers;

likewise, for one to whom this *prajñāpāramitā* is within reach of the hand due to being fit for grasping, he will before long obtain supreme enlightenment—the *saṃbhogakāya*—here through the power of the application of hearing and so forth from the Leaders. (7)

He also speaks by way of describing the activity of offering the *nirmāṇakāya*, beginning with "Just as," and so forth: Just as a woman who is somewhat despicable, being pregnant because she has conceived a fetus, when she moves about with her limbs stretching due to the proximity of the time of birth and is overcome by pains, then it should be known that this is the time for her to give birth, for the sake of procreation.

Likewise, when a bodhisattva, hearing and reflecting upon the perfection of wisdom of the Victors as previously described, manifests zeal through the application of ever-increasing aspiration, then, by attaining the practice of hearing and so forth, he will swiftly touch enlightenment and the realization of the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya). // 8 //

How is it that through hearing and so forth, the dharmas to be abandoned and the dharmas to be adopted are obtained by way of relinquishment and acquisition? To this he says: "While practicing," and so on. Because the yogin, while practicing through hearing and so forth in the supreme perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), does not perceive the increase or arising of the forms of all phenomena in reality, nor their decrease or destruction; therefore, he perceives these dharmas and non-dharmas as having attained mere appearance, [seeing] the *dharmadhātu* as being like an illusion.

Because its essence is the gnosis whose core is emptiness and compassion, one does not touch upon extinction—the awakening of the śrāvakas and so forth—by the power of practice in accordance with reality as it is. And he who dwells [in this state] does so through the performance of the dharmas for attaining the three bodies within the wisdom described above; thus, from the cultivation of the non-erroneous path, all of this will be the fruit. Therefore, the thought is that the applications must be undertaken. 9.

Because their greatness is proclaimed with particular excellence, even without explicitly stating their qualities, the applications (*prayoga*) are practiced all the more thoroughly once they have been observed; therefore, in order to state their qualities, he says "the final atom," and so forth. While practicing the performance of the applications, the bodhisattva does not establish himself here [in a fixed state] during the cultivation of the aspects of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).

In general, he conceptualizes the Buddha-qualities as cause and fruit; specifically, he conceptualizes the powers (*bala*), such as faith and the rest; the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) accompanied by zeal and so forth—these being illustrative, he also includes the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and others as causes.

Furthermore, because all perversions have been stilled, he perceives awakening (*bodhi*) as the fruit, which is peaceful. This is because, through the power of application, he has realized that those things which have become objects for both non-conceptual and conceptual knowledge possess a nature established exclusively as being like an illusion, appearing in a false form.

Because he moves with sovereignty through the arising of qualities such as the destruction of Māra’s power by being free from conceptual construction and its proliferation, he becomes one who acts through empowerment; for this very reason, since it has the nature of the application of wisdom, it is the practice and performance of the supreme perfection. // 10 //
The tenth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Qualities of Retention," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthāvyākhyā*.
The eleventh chapter, "On the Deeds of Māra.

Immediately following the [discussion of] qualities, [the author] speaks of the faults that create obstacles to practice—those which must be abandoned so that practices may be cultivated—by saying "Buddham" and so forth. Subhūti questioned the Buddha, the Moon among Speakers, because his teaching of the Dharma removes the heat of delusion for the wise. He asked: "How many obstacles will there be for those who delight in the application of qualities, since these qualities are the cause of virtue? This is the question.
"There will be many obstacles; therefore, I shall first describe only a small portion by way of illustration"—this is the Teacher's rebuttal. 1.

He says this very thing with the words beginning "insights" (*pratibhāna*). Various kinds of insights, consisting of distinguished forms of knowledge regarding the Mother, will arise. However, because this perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—which consists of the written text and its meaning—is not made firm through the investigation of the sequence of the Conquerors' teachings, those insights will quickly vanish again and again like lightning. For the sake of the world that has failed to achieve its goal, this is an activity of Māra; for some, even a doubt or hesitation regarding the reality spoken by the Buddha may arise here.

When this [teaching] is being spoken, because of a lack of full understanding, [the listener will think]: "Since my name has not been proclaimed here by the Blessed One, nor has my birthplace or lineage been proclaimed, he will certainly not listen; rather, he will reject it, saying, 'This is not the word of the Buddha. This too is the work of Māra. (2–3)

To the question "What will they do then?", he says "In this way," and so forth. Thus, those persons influenced by Māra, having abandoned the root—the primary cause—because they lack the realization of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtabodha*) due to their ignorance, will seek out the Sūtras of the Śrāvakas and others, which are like branches and leaves. Just as some who desire an elephant, having already found one, go searching for the elephant's footprint, so too, having heard the *Prajñāpāramitā*, they will search for other Sūtras.

Just as someone who has obtained food of a hundred flavors might seek out sixty-day-old rice, and having obtained it, considers that to be the best of foods—this is the intended meaning—so too, a bodhisattva, having obtained this perfection, will seek for the state of an Arhat, and therein he will conceive the notion that it is the essence; such is the remainder of the sense. (4–5)

Explaining the deeds of Māra by way of another method, he says: "Desirous of honor," and so forth. Because they long for mere reputation, they will be desirous of honor; because they seek wealth, they will be desirous of gain; because they look toward requisites, they will be full of expectations; and because of living in association with householders for the sake of alms-food and the like, they will be engaged in intimacy and familiarity with families. Having abandoned this Dharma which is their mother, because of the presence of only a slight amount of Dharma, they will perform activities such as those of the non-Dharma Śrāvaka vehicle; having left the path, they will be like those who have gone onto a wrong road—this is the deed of Māra.

Furthermore, at that time, those who—out of a desire to hear this supreme Dharma, the mother of the future Victors, and through their conviction in the results of karma—will generate faith; yet, having recognized the Dharma-preacher, they will speak unkindly out of their own [preconceived] intentions. Because their faith has departed and their affection is removed, they will go elsewhere, deprived of the attainment of the sought-after goal and being ill-disposed toward the True Dharma. This too is the work of Māra. (6–7)

Since it is impossible to describe them in every way due to their infinity, he concludes by pointing out a portion of the deeds of Māra, saying: "These are the deeds of Māra," and so forth. These are those deeds of Māra mentioned above; they will arise in that future time, or in other times, as many various kinds of obstacles and hindrances produced by creating such impediments.

The meaning is this: because many monks at that time were distracted and agitated by those faults due to their acquisition of mental distraction, they did not uphold this Perfection of Wisdom—lacking both the retention of its text and its meaning—while others, such as lay practitioners (upāsakas) and so forth, certainly did not uphold it even more so. // 8 //

To the question "Why is there much adversity? he says: "Those which exist," and so forth. Those jewels which exist are beyond price because they have transcended all value; being difficult to obtain, they are hard to acquire. By their very nature (*dharmatā*), they are desired by everyone and thus always have many adversaries. In the same way, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is a rare jewel of the Dharma for the Victors, and it would likewise be beset by much adversity. (9)

Is this *māra*-activity [present] for everyone? No; he says "those who have newly set out in the vehicle," and so forth. Because they have only recently begun, those bodhisattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle possess very little merit and thus have limited intelligence; by the power of being influenced by Māra, they will not obtain this Mother, this rare jewel of the Dharma. If that is so, and since it is impossible for all [to obtain it] at the outset, does it follow that there is no attainment at all? To this he says: "Māra is here," and so forth.

Although Māra, having become agitated by the thought, "How shall I create an obstacle here in this Mother of the Victors? will be eager to engage in an interruption that would sever her activity, nevertheless, the Blessed Buddhas established in the ten directions—having accumulated great merit—attend to the protection of the Mother; because they are engaged in providing her with a protector, there is the attainment of her, which is to say, her "going" (gati). // 10 //
The eleventh chapter, on the Deeds of Māra, in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*.
The twelfth chapter, "The Manifestation to the World.

Explaining by means of an analogy why it is that the Blessed Ones attend [to them] alone, he says "Mother," and so forth: Just as when a mother has many sons, they all become dejected at her illness and apply themselves with effort, out of gratitude, to removing obstacles such as fever and the like; [so too do the Buddhas act].

In the same way, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are established throughout the world-systems in the ten directions, take heed of this Mother Prajñāpāramitā by means of their exertion in acknowledging what has been done for them and in dispelling the obstacles of Māra’s deeds. Since the characteristics have already been explained, one should cultivate the practices determined through the gateway of the knowledge of characteristics, preceded by the adoption of virtues and the abandonment of faults.

In that regard, first of all, by means of the adoption of the instrument for producing cognition (*matikaraṇa*), threefold characteristics—namely, cognition (*jñāna*), the specific [object], and activity (*kāritra*)—are characterized. By relying on the instrumental derivation (*karmasādhana*) of the word "that" (*tad*), there is a fourth characteristic, which is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). // 1 //

In that regard, first concerning the characteristic of knowledge—which is divided according to the three types of omniscience—he speaks, by way of the gateway of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), regarding the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa and so forth, beginning with the words "Those who [have passed] beyond... and so on.

Moreover, those Blessed Lords, the Protectors of the World, who exist currently in the ten directions, have all been born from this Mother, the Perfection of Wisdom, through the practice of sequential application; they are being born now, and those of the future will also be born from her. Furthermore, because she reveals the reality of things as they truly are, she is the "showing one" for the world; because she causes growth, she is the "progenitor"; because she brings them forth, she is the "mother" of all beings; and because she understands the mental conduct of others, she is the "revealer" of the mental conduct of other sentient beings.

Because he is engaged through the power of applying the non-erroneous path, the appearance of the Tathāgatas occurs; yet, as for how [there can be] the manifestation of the world and so forth given its infinity, he says "of the world" and so on. The suchness (*tathatā*) of the world—that is, the realm of sentient beings—which, due to its being like an illusion, is the suchness of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, is the very same suchness of the Tathāgatas, because there is no distinction between each individual term or the limiting conditions of objects.

Because the Blessed One does not perceive any difference in essential nature [between himself and others], he is non-different from the *prajñāpāramitā* which serves as the cause; thus, through the realization of the state of things (*bhāvagammat*) within non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*), they are Buddhas. Since it is logically impossible for anything to exist apart from the *dharmadhātu*, the Tathāgata perceives the world and so forth; otherwise, it would be impossible to establish the state of omniscience—this is the intended meaning. (3)

Immediately following that, in order to explain the characteristics of the knowledge of emptiness and so forth by way of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), he says: "They abide," and so on. Because this *dharmatā*—the nature of phenomena as a fixed order of things—is established for the Blessed Ones who abide in the present, those who are world-knowers in the future, and those who have attained final nirvāṇa in the past; otherwise, because it would be contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and would thus take the form of error, liberation would be impossible. That is to say, since all phenomena are empty, therefore [he speaks of] that.

By virtue of having practiced the application, Bodhisattvas realize suchness—which is the very nature of the knowledge of emptiness and so forth—as reality through its non-alterity (*anyathārthena*). And precisely because they have realized all phenomena through this awakening to suchness, the Tathāgatas bestow upon the Sons of the Conquerors the name "Buddhas. // 4 //

If this is so, one might ask: how can there be the welfare of sentient beings for them in the knowledge of emptiness and so forth? To this he says: "This domain is tenfold," and so on. This realization of the uncommon dharma becomes a "domain" (*gocara*) because it has entered the state of being an object; it belongs only to the Sons of the Conquerors (*jinaputra*), the Guides (*vināyaka*) who possess the ten powers, because the *prajñāpāramitā* is pleasing to their minds. It should be understood as having resorted to a mountain, because it is delightful and because it occupies an exceedingly lofty position.

That is to say, by means of the manifestation of great compassion, they uplift those sentient beings who suffer from the perversions of birth and so forth, delivering them from the three lower realms such as the hells through the teaching of dharmas such as emptiness; yet, due to their perfection of the knowledge of emptiness and so forth, they never harbor even the slightest notion of a "sentient being. // 5 //

To the question, "How can one who is attached to apprehension be disciplined by the teaching of dharmas such as emptiness? he says: "Just as a lion... and so forth. Likewise, a lion, relying on a certain part of a mountain cave, emits a roar intended to produce fear.

Being himself free from all fear, he is undaunted; like a lion frightening small deer in his own domain, the Bodhisattva—being a lion among men—utters his roar by teaching the Dharma of emptiness and so forth, endowed with unimpeded measure, having relied upon the Perfection of Wisdom which provides no foothold for those who perceive objects. Being undaunted because of the absence of apprehension, and frightening the many heretics—who, due to their attachment to a self and so forth, lack liberation—he thereby disciplines them; such is the meaning. // 6 //

Immediately following that, in order to explain the characteristics of the knowledge consisting of the dwelling based on one's own dharma and so forth by way of the gateway of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he says: "Just as space," and so on. Just as the sun, depending upon space, with its thousands of rays, heats this earth with water and heat, and reveals the true nature of all things by removing darkness; likewise, through the state of practiced application, relying upon the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)—which is the dwelling based on one's own dharma—by means of the knowledge of the dwellings and so forth, [one proceeds] by the right path.

By establishing [the Dharma] through the observance of rules, the Blessed One, King of Dharma, causes the river of craving—which brings about the world's obstruction, desiccation, and suffering—to dry up; and having ascertained the Dharmas, he demonstrates them through practice. // 7 //

To explain how there is the vision of phenomena (*dharma*), he says "form," and so forth. Since all phenomena are subsumed within the five aggregates, the vision of form is that in which it does not exist at all because it is like an illusion. Likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—consciousness being called "mind" (*citta*) because it is the locus of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of wholesome and other phenomena. And the non-vision of that [mind] is where there is no vision, due to its being devoid of a nature that is either one or many. This very non-vision is what the Tathāgata has taught as the vision of phenomena with the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*).

Therefore, for one who has turned away from error, non-seeing is indeed said to be seeing—due to the deficiency of conditions, like those with closed eyes or those blind from birth, or due to a lack of mental attention. Consequently, the view is that for the yogin who has emerged from the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth, there arises the obscuration of afflictions and the knowable (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*), characterized by the attachment to existence and non-existence and by indolence. // 8 //

What is this "seeing" that is the non-seeing of phenomena? He says: "Like space," and so forth. Just as space—being merely the absence of all substantial entities—is said by beings to be "unseen" because it transcends the scope of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) such as direct perception and inference, and yet they employ it in conventional discourse; [so too is the seeing of phenomena].

Furthermore, since space does not exist in reality, it has been described as a vision in the form of a certain and absolute [non-existence]. Therefore, through this logical analysis, you should investigate this matter: understand that the conventional expression "vision of space" is in fact non-vision, because it is the exhaustion of vision.

Thus, the Tathāgata has taught that the very non-vision of phenomena is their vision; for it is impossible to speak of a vision by way of a vision that is certain and absolute in form, because all things are like an illusion (*māyopama*). // 9 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the twelfth chapter, "The Manifestation of the World."
The thirteenth chapter, "The Inconceivable.

Since the specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) must be explained as that which is to be known (*jñeya*) as a particularity among those things already delimited by way of their general form through the aspects of knowledge (*jñānākāra*), and since that [specific characteristic] consists of the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) distinguished from the paths of the Śrāvakas and others, it should be understood as characterized by the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth, having as its objects the truths of suffering and the rest, and being distinguished by particularities such as the inconceivable. Thus he says, "Whosoever," and so on: the Bodhisattva who perceives the Mother (the Perfection of Wisdom) by means of mental attention through these very aspects, such as the inconceivable and the incomparable.

Through the power of application (*prayoga-bala*), he perceives here, by virtue of his realization, that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*)—by way of their specific characteristics and intrinsic nature—are [subsumed] within the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth, because all activity is bound up therein. Just as a minister performs all tasks while the king remains indifferent, so too does the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) perform all those activities; for, since the term "Buddha" is a general designation, it includes the functional qualities of the perfectly enlightened ones (*samyaksambuddha*), the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddha*), and likewise those of the disciples (*śrāvaka*). // 1 //

Clarifying this very point, he says "And not," and so forth. Just as that king does not go to [other] kings such as those of Videha, nor to countries such as Magadha, nor to kingdoms such as Rājagṛha, but rather, while traveling from his own realm, gives everything away; in the same way, the Bodhisattva, established in the nature of reality (dharmatā), does not move anywhere, yet he gives away all those qualities—such as the patience regarding the knowledge of phenomena concerning suffering—which have the nature of the path of distinction up to the stage of Buddhahood. // 2 //
The thirteenth chapter, "The Inconceivable," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*.
The fourteenth chapter, "The Chapter on Similes.

Now, [the author] asks: when, specifically, are the qualities of a Buddha attained? He says: "If there is," and so forth. If there is faith—based on the statement that a Buddha is one who possesses the qualities that constitute a Buddha—and if, toward the Sugata, there exists through the Buddha-qualities a firm conviction regarding the reality of the antidotes to opposing factors, and if there exists the application of the Bodhisattva’s excellent and superior resolve in conjunction with the intention (*āśaya*) for the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), then, because it proceeds without transgressing the two truths, having transcended the two stages (*bhūmi*).

One will swiftly attain the awakening that is the cause of the awakening of the Victors—those who are not overcome by Māra, the heretics, and others—and which possesses the characteristic of distinction, [attaining it] beyond the reach of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, it may be said that one should apply intense practice toward the objects of faith and wisdom; however, this is not because faith is the precursor to all dharmas. // 1 //

To explain how the function of wisdom operates here, he provides a response by means of an analogy, through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), beginning with the words "sāmudrī" and so forth: "Just as when a sea-going ship is wrecked, a person who is dying will meet his destruction in the midst of the water without reaching the shore, provided he does not grasp at any support such as grass or wood; whereas he who grasps at a corpse or the like travels easily to the further shore and thus reaches dry land."

In the very same way, those who have approached with faith but, out of mere superficial clarity, abandon the Mother Prajñāpāramitā because she is without objective support, then wander forever in the ocean of saṃsāra due to the difficulty of subduing the suffering of passion and the like. Because they have not abandoned their cognitive distortions through mere faith alone, they continue to transmigrate. Birth is arising; aging is the state of decay; death is the cessation of one's own category of existence; and dejection resulting from separation from children, wife, and so forth is sorrow (*śoka*). These are the waves in that ocean of saṃsāra, and its "breaking" refers to the destruction of those [waves]; thus it is described as such, and the phrase "in that" should be applied accordingly.

Furthermore, those who possess the power of faith and are embraced by excellent wisdom—being skilled in [the nature of] phenomena because they understand that the intrinsic nature of things is like an illusion, and because they perceive even Nirvāṇa through the power of the principle of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda)—are seers of the ultimate truth. By the power of their faith and wisdom, they possess, respectively, the complete accumulation of merit and knowledge, which consists of the nature of the vehicles, the vessels, and the stages beginning with the Joyous (pramuditā). This is what exists for them.
