Having been described in this way, they likewise quickly touch the most wonderful enlightenment of the Sugatas, which is not within the sphere of the Śrāvakas and others. Therefore, it may be said that one who seeks the specific characteristics [of the path] must take both as their object without interruption. Furthermore, the examples of "having an object" and "not having an object" are given according to the case, in order to illustrate the presence of the opposing factors for those who practice with or without interruption. (2-4)

Having explained that these two alone are the distinguished basis, he says "the jar," and so forth, as before: Just as one carries water with an unripened jar, one should know that when [certain conditions] exist, this [jar] will quickly fail; because it is weak and incapable of carrying a great volume of water, it breaks. But by carrying water with a ripened jar, one does not encounter the fear of breaking on the road; furthermore, because it is connected to what lies ahead, one goes safely to home without any intermediate calamity.

Likewise, even though the faithful one, while fully embracing [the path], might transcend the wisdom characterized by the investigation of phenomena (dharmavicaya) and attain supreme enlightenment by reaching the two stages of the Śrāvakas and others through the acquisition of the special path (viśeṣamārga), [this would still not be sufficient]. // 5-6 //

The two rotten vessels (*aghaṭau*) are intended to demonstrate the state of being a receptacle for the qualities of practice and non-practice, respectively. Now, one might ask: "If other things can also serve as receptacles, why these two alone? In response, [the author] says "not a ship" (*nāva*) and so forth, providing an answer based on their preeminence. Just as a ship that has not been repaired by removing rotten wood and the like goes to destruction in the great ocean along with its cargo and its merchants;

And that very ship, having been well-prepared and being driven by a favorable wind, remains well-yoked, does not leak, and reaches the shore carrying its cargo. In the same way, a bodhisattva who is permeated with faith but lacks wisdom falls away easily from unsurpassed awakening before reaching final nirvāṇa; he suffers decline. Yet that same bodhisattva, being permeated with faith and being properly yoked to the excellent perfection of wisdom, remains uninjured because there is no falling into other [lower] states.

And because it is correctly engaged in its own vehicle, it is unimpaired; in that very way, it touches the awakening of the Victors. Thus, it is made known that there is only a pair for the sake of the completeness of practice. Regarding those things that have been struck and those that have been polished, there is no further grasping; this very pair is "complete possession" for the purpose of making known the completeness of both practice and non-practice. (7–8)

He says the same thing in the passage beginning with "For a man," and so forth. Just as a certain man, being old with limbs worn out by decrepitude, suffering from a lack of food and other necessities, and being over two hundred years old, might rise up from his seat on his own; yet, due to the absence of assistance and being incapable, he is unable to go even a *krośa* or half a *krośa*. When he is supported by men grasping both his left and right arms, then there is no fear of falling.

Just as one travels with ease to the place that is to be reached, even so, because of a lack of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in wisdom, a weak bodhisattva here, although he sets out to go by means of mere faith, nevertheless breaks down midway; for, being deprived of the assistance of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), he is broken by falling into the level of the śrāvakas and others.

When that very [element] is embraced by excellent wisdom (*prajñā*) which serves as the means (*upāya*), it is then not destroyed; rather, through the attainment of the specific characteristics, one touches the awakening (*bodhi*) of the Blessed Ones, the bulls among men. Therefore, the illustration of the old man being either embraced or not embraced is intended to demonstrate, according to the circumstances, how one might fall exclusively into either cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) or nirvāṇa, depending on whether or not one is embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*). Thus it should be understood. The fourteenth chapter, "The Chapter on Similes," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*.
The fifteenth chapter, "The Chapter on the Gods.

Regarding the attainment of the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) according to the principle already stated, he says "those who," etc., to show that one should not indulge in the perception of [faults] due to the power of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Those bodhisattvas who, because they have first set out by means of the specific characteristics, abide on the stage of the beginner (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*); who, because they possess auspicious qualities, have set out for the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*); and who, because they do not grasp at faults, are good disciples who please [their teachers] through great respect and are endowed with reverence for their gurus.
The wise should serve spiritual friends at all times through attendance and other such means, for the sake of protecting their own minds. (1)

Regarding the question of what the cause for serving a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is, he says: "For what reason? In response, he says: "Because from them," and so forth. Because from those spiritual friends there comes the attainment of qualities characterized by excellence; and because, through their instructions and admonitions, there is the experience [of the Dharma] and the absence of [conceptual] apprehension, those spiritual friends instruct the wise disciples and those [practitioners] of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Therefore, the Jina has spoken thus: because he has abandoned all obscurations and possesses the highest of all qualities, the Buddha-qualities—which have the nature of specific characteristics—exist by relying upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Thus, it is the conviction that those [friends] are to be served. // 2 //

To explain what their instruction and admonition (*avavādānuśāsanī*) is like, he says: "And generosity," and so forth. Because all phenomena are subsumed within generosity and the other perfections, the six perfections—which otherwise proceed by way of apprehension (*upalambha*)—must be dedicated toward awakening for its sake, by means of the non-apprehension of object, agent, and action; this is because they would otherwise undergo a transformation of form, and thus one must abandon the apprehension of savoring them.

Furthermore, the aggregates of awakening are not distinct from the aggregates of morality and so forth that constitute the fruit free from outflows; for they are established through reasoning. Having reflected upon this, one subsequently does not experience relish through the condition of grasping at them, thinking, "one who would grasp [them as real]. Moreover, the teaching must indeed be given to those beginners who have first applied themselves, by means of a definitive realization of their illusion-like nature through reasoning; otherwise, due to a lack of conviction, they would fall into terror—this is the intended meaning. // 3 //

Having explained the accomplishment of one’s own welfare through the description of the specific characteristics of knowledge, [the author], now describing the accomplishment of the welfare of others through the application of practices characterized by the performance of benefit and so forth, says "In this way," and so on. Precisely because of their thorough understanding of the specific characteristics of knowledge, Bodhisattvas who proceed in such applications through the power of cultivation are "oceans of qualities" because they provide future happiness through the teaching of the Dharma, being themselves of unfathomable virtue; or they are "moons among speakers" because they bring satisfaction by bestowing present happiness.

They are "protectors" (*trāṇa*) in the world of sentient beings because they provide benefit by establishing [beings] in the state of perfect non-ripening (*avipāka-dharmatā*). Likewise, they are "refuges" (*śaraṇa*) because they produce ultimate welfare and are not to be relied upon [by others]; they are "shelters" (*layana*) because they are resorted to for the purpose of turning back from the causes of suffering; and they are "destinations and understandings" (*gatibuddhi*) because, through the awakening to the equality of *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*, they are the cause of the intellect that is intent upon reaching the supreme excellence.

They are "islands" because, through their function as the basis for realization, they provide the self-benefit and benefit-for-others that are delimited by the two extremes, in analogy with dry land surrounded by water. They are "guides" because, by virtue of being essential supports, they bring about the practice for the benefit of others. They are "benefactors" because, by providing for the welfare of beings engaged in enjoyments through emanations, they accomplish what is beneficial. They are "luminous torches" because, by teaching the direct realization of the departure via all vehicles, they create light upon the path to enlightenment.

Because he relies upon the teaching of the reality of all phenomena, he is a speaker of the sublime Dharma; for that very reason, because he cannot be disturbed by Māra, the non-Buddhists, and others, he is immovable. // 4 //

Having thus understood their nature through the very fact that they must accomplish the fulfillment of the welfare of both self and others, he speaks of the definition of their essential nature by first describing the character of their practice, saying: "I am not existent," and so forth. Because it is accomplished through effort (*prayatna*), I am not "existent" (*san*). Because it is performed with difficulty, the nature of these applications is "difficult to perform" (*duṣkara*). Because they have attained great majesty, the Bodhisattvas are "of great resolve" (*mahāśaya*). Those who, from the commencement of cultivation, gird themselves for battle [are the Bodhisattvas].

Because there is no perception of opposing factors (*vipakṣa*), they are not armored by the five aggregates (*skandha*), nor by the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), nor by the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*). Because they are free from attachment to remedies (*pratipakṣa*), they are devoid of the three notions associated with the Śrāvakas and others; and because they are thus separated from the grasping at phenomena as things to be abandoned or accepted, they are "unappropriated" (*aparigṛhīta*). Because there is no opening for the fulfillment of their own welfare (*svārthasaṃpad*), they are "irreversible" (*avaivartika*);

because the fulfillment of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpad*) cannot be shaken, they are "immovable" (*acalita*); and because it is impossible to alter the fulfillment of both, they possess "unchanging qualities" (*akopyadharmāṇaḥ*). // 5 //

He explains how they are relevant to the present context with the words "ta" and so forth: "Those very ones mentioned by Ananta, through the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), are endowed with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) characterized by the separation from afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth regarding the applications (*prayoga*); they are free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) due to the attainment of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*). Because they are devoid of doubt, false, and erroneous cognition, they are free from hesitation, distress, and indecision. Being possessed of perfect knowledge, they are endowed with the ultimate goal."

Having heard the *prajñāpāramitā*, because they possess firm conviction (*saṃpratyaya*) in realization, they do not despond; for this very reason, they are to be known as "not led by others" (*aparapraṇeya*) and as "irreversible" (*avaivartika*) due to the absence of turning back from their own state. // 6 //

He says "profound," and so forth, to show that such a nature cannot be realized in all its aspects by anyone other than a Tathāgata. Because it is like an illusion, this profound dharma—the nature belonging to the Blessed Ones—is difficult to realize and difficult to see; it has not been realized in all its aspects by any other, such as a Śrāvaka, nor does anyone realize it now, nor will anyone realize it in the future.

Because of its profundity, for this very purpose, the Blessed One—having attained enlightenment through the incidental realization of Tathāgatahood by prioritizing the welfare of sentient beings—remains compassionate and intent on the benefit of all people. This is because it would be logically untenable [to explain the path] without the characteristic of the nature of the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Because he had become one of little concern due to the withdrawal from the welfare of sentient beings—thinking, "Who will understand this Dharma as it is being taught regarding its essential characteristics? Indeed, because of their attachment to apprehension (*upalambha*), no class of sentient beings [will understand it]"—he did not set his mind upon teaching the Dharma. Nevertheless, the intention is that at the request of Brahmā, he set the wheel of Dharma in motion. // 7 //

If this is so, how then is the attainment of the Dharma by sentient beings? To this he says: "And sentient beings," and so forth. Although sentient beings—being attached to passion and the like within the *ālayavijñāna* because they fail to see their faults due to the conceit of pleasure and so on; being established in the grasping [of objects] as seekers of sense-objects because they do not abandon mental attention to them due to seeing qualities in them; being ignorant through the application of nescience (*ajñāna*) because of the presence of doubt-knowledge; and being blinded by the presence of false knowledge due to self-love—nevertheless, the Dharma has the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because it is the antidote to the practice of passion and so forth, it is "without abode" (*anālaya*); because it acts to uproot the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is "without grasping" (*anāgraha*). Since this conflict with the world—characterized by being overwhelmed by perversions—is that which must be brought about for people by the Buddhas and others, it has appeared through the teaching of the five aggregates and so forth as being unimpeded and selfless, according to the analogy of reporting the death of a queen to the king on earth. // 8 //
The fifteenth chapter, "The Gods," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*.
The sixteenth chapter, "Suchness.

If it is argued that the nature of the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) is differentiated because it is realized through non-differentiated knowledge with respect to each sentient being, [the author] says "no," beginning with the words "like space" (*ākāśa*). Just as the element of space is of one form in the eastern direction, so it is in the southern, so in the western, and so in the northern direction, and likewise above and below; because it is without distinction and lacks any intrinsic reality (*tattva*), it is infinite.

Likewise, throughout all ten directions, as far as the element of space extends, there would be no diversity because it lacks a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); and due to its separation from a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there would be no attainment of distinction. (1)

Having pointed out the example by means of worldly renown, he also speaks by means of supramundane realization, beginning with "transcended," and so forth: that which is the suchness (*tathatā*) of things past that have transcended; that which is the suchness of future things yet to be attained; that which is the suchness of present, current things; that which is the suchness of Arhats by virtue of having exhausted the outflows (*kṣīṇāsrava*); and, by contrast with that, the suchness of all phenomena.

And that suchness which belongs to all the Blessed Ones, as just described, is the suchness consisting of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); because there is no differentiation in liberation, and due to the absence of any valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a distinction, it does not attain any particularity. Likewise, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the applications (*prayoga*) is considered to be one alone, since it is directly realized by many. // 2 //

Since the thorough knowledge of the characteristics as they have been described is like the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), he says "The bodhisattva who... and so forth, in order to speak of those [roots] conducive to liberation: The bodhisattva who desires to attain through direct realization the enlightenment of the Sugatas—which is devoid of the various phenomena because of the absence of all apprehension—[practices] for the sake of the full accomplishment of the Buddha-qualities such as generosity and the rest, by means of the mode of non-apprehension through signless knowledge.

Through the thorough knowledge of all aspects, one should possess the entire range of beings within the Perfection of Wisdom by means of qualities such as supreme faith and so forth. For, without wisdom—which serves as the defining characteristic of these qualities—there is no realization for those who lead men [to liberation]. (3)

"Now, since there are indeed other means for attaining Buddhahood, why are only the two—wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*)—taught? Anticipating this objection, he provides a refutation by means of an analogy, beginning with the words "the bird," and so forth: "Just as a bird might have a great body, measuring hundreds of *yojanas* and more, yet be weak because its wings are not yet grown at fifty *yojanas*, and furthermore, its wings might be exhausted because they are still covered [by feathers]."

If one were to cast oneself down from the abode of the Trāyastriṃśa gods with the intention, "I shall stay here in Jambudvīpa," then upon falling, one would meet destruction due to the deficiency of wings. Likewise, even if one were to fully accomplish these five perfections—generosity and the rest—of the Victors over many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, and were to cultivate them extensively through the practice of vast aspirations that are manifold and infinite, and by means of extensive applications to the objects of the Dharma; [without the wings of wisdom, one will not reach the goal].

Nevertheless, due to the absence of the previously mentioned means (*upāya*), one is "without means"; and due to the absence of dwelling in wisdom (*prajñā*) as described, one is "devoid of wisdom. Because of this deficiency in both wings, one would fall into the state of a *śrāvaka*, and consequently perish on the stage of unsurpassed [enlightenment]. Thus, it is precisely these two—wisdom and means—that are shown to be primary. (4–5)

In order to speak of the factors of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), he says: "For the sake of entering into the certainty" (*niyāmāvakrāntaye*), and so forth. That bodhisattva who here rightly desires to set out toward the attainment of the heat (*ūṣman*) and the other stages for the sake of the Buddha-knowledge, should first exert himself for the purpose of generating the heat; because of the absence of attachment, he is even-minded. Because he dwells upon the entire world as his object of focus (*ālambana*), he should exert himself. Thus, because he regards them as fathers, he has the perception of fatherhood; because he regards them as mothers, he has the perception of motherhood; because he knows their future welfare, he is benevolent in mind (*hita-citta*); and because he brings the present welfare before his mind, he is friendly in mind (*maitra-citta*)—thus he should exert himself.

Because he is free from the faults of resentment and malice, he is "entire" (*akhila*); because his mind is like that toward brothers, sisters, and so forth, he is "straightforward" (*ārjava*). The phrase "should exert himself" (*parākrāmet*) is to be connected with what precedes. For the sake of attaining the stages beginning with the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), he should always speak with gentle words, being intent on personal practice and engaging others in virtue and so forth by means of such address.

If it is asked, "How is it that the designation 'aids to penetration' (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so forth is appropriate here, given that this is of the nature of the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*)?"—it is said: [73b] By virtue of attaining the path of effortless signlessness on the eighth [stage], in order to avoid the interruption of the welfare of sentient beings for that duration, and in order to refute [the notion of] simultaneous arising, the very path of distinction—which arises through aspects such as equanimity of mind and by taking sentient beings as its object through the likeness to an illusion—is what is intended here by the designation "aids to penetration" and so forth, as it arises in the sequence of weak, medium, and so on.
Likewise, it should be understood that even further on, [the same applies] as far as possible. // 6 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthāvyākhyā*, the sixteenth chapter, "On Suchness" (*tathatā*), is concluded.
The seventeenth chapter is the "Chapter on Irreversibility. Regarding the community of irreversible bodhisattvas:

since there are not only the aforementioned aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) but also other stages such as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth, the community of irreversible bodhisattvas must be described. That [community] is established as follows: those situated on the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) consisting of the aids to penetration; likewise, those situated on the path of seeing comprised of receptivities (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*); and others situated on the continuous path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Therefore, asking about the general characteristics of irreversibility, he says, beginning with "O Elder," and so forth.

The Elder Subhūti questioned the Lord of the World regarding the physical sign that serves as the mark of death for one whose practice is unmixed due to the abandonment of the obscurations of doubt concerning oneself and others; by way of this illustration, the aspect, the antidote, the summarized characteristic, and the equipment are included.

Speak once more, O Blessed Ones, by means of a single utterance: because the sons of the Victors possess bodies composed of immeasurable qualities, they are those for whom there is no turning back from supreme enlightenment due to their accumulation of virtues; tell us by what signs and so forth they are endowed. Since Bodhisattvas are of great majesty through their union with the perfection of the welfare of themselves and others, please explain that sign and so forth clearly through a detailed exposition. O Victor, O Blessed One, since you intend to speak in extreme brevity, [this is] merely a partial indication of the qualities, such as the cessation of form and so forth. (1)

In that regard, first, in order to state the characteristics of non-retrogression for those abiding in the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), he says "free from diversity" (*nānātva*) and so forth. Because they have turned away from grasping at form and the other [sense objects], they are free from the perception of diversity (*nānātvasaṃjñā*).

Because they utter speech that is consistent with the goal by way of illuminating the meaning that is like an illusion, they are speakers of reasoned words; because they have abandoned doubt, they do not seek refuge in other [non-Buddhist] ascetics (*śramaṇas*), such as the Paṇḍara-bhikṣus, or in Brahmins, through acts of taking refuge and the like. Because they are free from the eight unfavorable conditions—these being indicative of the three lower realms—and because they are devoid of wrong views and so forth, they are wise, possessing full knowledge of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and they exist at all times.

Because they establish both themselves and others exclusively in the abstention from taking life and so forth, those sons of the Conquerors are endowed with the ten wholesome paths of action. Through the dedication of the perfections such as generosity toward the realm of all sentient beings, they instruct the world with a mind free from worldly motives by not looking for rewards such as fruits; and because they are devoid of doubt even regarding the profound Dharma, they are resolutely delighted in the single Dharma that is like an illusion.

Because they possess bodily, vocal, and mental actions endowed with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they always speak with affectionate words since they express what is beneficial and pleasant. Through the application of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*samprajanya*), they know how to conduct themselves beautifully and correctly in standing, walking, lying down, and sitting. They walk looking only a yoke’s length ahead in order to avoid places inhabited by living beings and the like. Because they are free from distraction, their deportment (*iryāpatha*) is unbroken and their minds are undeluded.

They are pure because they are dissociated from unwholesome states (*akuśaladharma*); they wear clean garments because they enjoy secluded clothing and the like; they are purified by the threefold seclusion because they have attained the purity of body, speech, and mind adorned with the [major] marks and so forth; they do not desire gain because they do not give rise to thoughts of stinginess and the like; they are preeminent bulls because they practice yoga that is never contrary to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and because they always desire the Dharma out of compassion for the world, even longing for the hells and other realms; and they have transcended the domain of Māra because they possess a firm conviction in the true nature of phenomena.

Because they have reached certainty regarding Māra even in the form of Māra, they are not led by others; because their conduct is authorized by the Buddhas, they meditate on the four dhyānas yet are not dependent upon those dhyānas. Immediately after the characteristics of irreversibility while abiding in the levels conducive to penetration, there are the characteristics of irreversibility for those who abide on the path of seeing through the cultivation of the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*). (2–4)

He says "and not," and so forth, in order to describe the activities of body, speech, and mind that correspond to that realization: because they have turned away from the perception of form and so on, they do not desire fame; because they are engaged in the Mahāyāna, they lack hatred toward anything and thus their minds are not overcome by anger; because they possess the skillful means for the welfare of sentient beings within the context of selflessness, they are unattached and have not become householders through the enjoyment of sensual desires; and because they practice celibacy by not viewing sense objects at all times, they are not intent upon any material things.

Because they possess the nature of a true person (*satpuruṣa*), they do not seek wealth through improper means such as buying and selling for the sake of a livelihood. Likewise, it should be understood that they do not seek out ritual applications (*prayogamantra*)—such as malevolent spells for Cāmuṇḍā and others for the purpose of harming sentient beings, nor the subjugation of women through mantras of Kāmadeva and so forth, nor the subjugation of men—because such mantras are contemptible. Furthermore, they do not prophesy based on bodily marks, saying, "Whether it be a man or a woman, this person will certainly become a performer of [sexual] acts."

By relying upon the two truths, they are devoted to discerning wisdom and the supreme perfection; being free from the exertion of body and speech, they are devoid of quarrels and disputes. Because their minds produce exceptional happiness for all sentient beings, they possess firm minds of loving-kindness. Because they abide in emptiness, they desire omniscience. Since there is no apprehension of even an atom of a phenomenon, they always have their minds inclined toward the teaching.

Because they have attained mastery over their own arising, they are free from birth there [in the lower realms]; thus, they are "avoided" by borderland barbarians, as the word "avoided" is also connected with what follows. Because they have abandoned the peripheral regions, they are "those who have avoided the peripheral regions. Because they have produced direct realization (*abhisampratyaya*), they are "free from doubt," since there is no uncertainty regarding their own stage (*svakabhūmi*), which consists of the three forms of omniscience. Because they abide in a state of certainty, they are "always like Mount Meru."

Because they have thoroughly internalized the meaning of the Dharma, such as omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), they sacrifice their lives by relinquishing their minds [to the Dharma]. Because they possess mental attention (*manasikāra*) that is immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), they are those who apply themselves to yoga. Because they desire to enter into even a single portion [of the path], they are those who infer the production of the complete effect through the cause of the non-retrogressive ones (*avaivartika*). According to the principle that "that which is described as an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) does not depend on other factors," these aforementioned signs (*liṅga*) are to be understood. (5–7)
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Aspects of Irreversibility."

The eighteenth chapter, "On Emptiness," begins by distinguishing the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—in order to explain the characteristics of the irreversible state situated on that path—according to the logical principle that "cognition does not arise toward a qualified object (*viśeṣya*) unless its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) has been grasped. Thus, he says "profound" (*gambhīra*), and so forth. Form (*rūpa*) is profound because it is, in reality, unarisen; likewise, feeling (*vedanā*), volition (*cetanā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and perception (*saṃjñā*) are profound. By this [statement], the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*), which holds that form and so forth exist within suchness (*tathatā*), is refuted.

Likewise, according to conventional truth, the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-svarūpa*) of form and the other aggregates is, by reason, signless (*animitta*) due to the departure of all signs; it is peaceful (*śānta*) due to the calming of all afflictions. By this, the extreme of denial—that *tathatā* is something other than form and the rest—is refuted.

Therefore, just as someone who has not found the bottom might search for a firm footing in the ocean by throwing a spear, so too, with wisdom free from the extremes of superimposition and denial regarding the aggregates, one should investigate through the condition of discernment; being one who has not yet found the bottom, because of its profound nature, it is said that the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is "profound. // 1 //

Having thus indicated the qualification along with its benefit, [the author], wishing to explain the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as the qualified object, asks by way of its activity, saying: "The one who, regarding awakening," and so forth. On that path of cultivation where, in reality, there are neither aggregates (*skandha*), nor sense-bases (*āyatana*), nor elements (*dhātu*), the Bodhisattva who repeatedly practices it attains these [objects] such as form (*rūpa*).

Because all phenomena are characterized by the selflessness of both phenomena and persons, they are untainted within the profound Mahāyāna due to the absence of any stain from the non-apprehension of ultimate reality; thus, it is "untainted. The meaning of the verse should be applied as follows: how much merit does such a person generate, and what is the extent of their attainment through the acquisition of the equipment of gnosis? // 2 //

If one were to explain the result (*phala*) by means of this, he says "just as" (*yathā*) and so forth: just as a certain man, whose temperament is characterized by passion (*rāga-dharma-carita*), because of his excessive attachment even toward a deficient object, makes an appointment after being told by a woman, "You must go with such-and-such a woman," and having gone there, finding her absent, thinks, "She has come here," and so on.

Thus, in this sequence, due to the abundance of discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), as many mental activities as there are that expand upon an object throughout the entire day—by turning his back on those [activities] for as many eons as are delimited by the number of a king’s movements and the thoughts of a man, the Bodhisattva awakens through the equipment of merit and knowledge (*puṇyajñānasambhāra*). The sense is that the equipment of merit and knowledge required for that awakening comes to be for him through the power of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Now, for the sake of abandoning the three types of conceptualization on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the distinction between its weak, medium, and intense modes must be explained, as a concise presentation is intended here. In this regard, it should be understood that the abandonment of intense conceptualization occurs by means of the weak path, up to the abandonment of weak conceptualization by means of the intense path; for an intense path cannot possibly exist from the very beginning, and once an intense path has arisen, there are no longer intense afflictions (*kleśa*).

Therefore, by demonstrating through other instructions that each subsequent [practice] possesses superior merit, and by means of the statement regarding the merit being overcome, the divisions of the counteracting factors (*pratipakṣa*) and the divisions of the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*) are indicated. // 3 //

To explain the meaning of the "gentle path," he says: "The bodhisattva who," and so forth. A bodhisattva who, for many thousands of millions of eons, gives gifts to the Buddhas and others by way of apprehension (*upalambha*), and who observes the morality associated with Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; and another son of the Conqueror (*jinaputra*) who is devoted to wisdom, the supreme perfection (*pāramitā*), which is the nature of the gentle path.

Then, having emerged from that state, one should correctly teach this Dharma to sentient beings; therefore, preceded by a distinguished mind, the gift of Dharma—when compared to this merit—is not even a fraction [of it], because one does not arise in a lowly state. This should be understood to apply to the previous gift as well, even when morality (*śīla*) is maintained, because the same principle applies here. // 4 //

He speaks for the sake of the meaning of the Middle Way, beginning with "he who," and so forth: that Bodhisattva who, having cultivated the excellent wisdom whose intrinsic nature is the Middle Way, and having emerged from that [meditative state], should preach the Dharma; [this Dharma is] "unstained" because of the absence of all defilements.

And one should dedicate even that taught Dharma toward awakening itself, which serves as the primary cause and the fundamental basis for the attainment of the welfare characterized by the prosperity and ultimate bliss of all beings. It should be understood that the merit arising from such dedication of the gift of Dharma, and whatever auspiciousness might accrue along with it, does not exist anywhere in the three worlds. // 5 //

He speaks of the superior path with the words "and from this" (*taś caiñ cāiva*), and so forth. When all that merit manifests again through the power of cultivating the path as it has been described, it is said [to be] "void" (*śūnyaka*) because it is devoid of imagined form; likewise, it is "insubstantial" (*tucchaka*) because of the absence of the nature of dharmatā due to dwelling in conceptually constructed phenomena. Even so, by way of conventional truth, it appears "powerless" (*vaśika*) because its arising is dependent on causes, and "pithless" (*asāraka*) because it is illusory in nature.

Thus, practicing in this way, one courses in the wisdom of the Sugatas, which has the nature of the supreme path; because it is non-erroneous, by practicing thus, one acquires immeasurable merit. However, in reality, it is not the case that through the power of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), the abandonment and attainment of the adverse factors and their remedies—respectively, that which is to be discarded and that which is to be adopted—are logically established. // 6 //

If it is asked, "In what way, then, is this so for the sons of the Victors? he says: "Merely through desire," and so forth. Because their intrinsic nature is mere designation, these phenomena—consisting of the mild, medium, and intense types—are merely objects of desire; for they are directed toward the accomplishment of one's own welfare, the welfare of others, or both.

Because they are ascertained by the means of valid cognition—direct perception, inference, and scripture—the Bodhisattva who, through the practice of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the arising of knowledge from hearing and so forth, understands these [teachings] as they have been taught, applied, and revealed by you respectively, over many millions of billions of eons while being spoken, does not diminish because the *dharmadhātu* and the state of a Victor (*jinatā*) are of a single flavor due to the removal of their opposites (*vipakṣa*). Nor does reality (*tattva*) increase due to the absence of the arising of its counteragent (*pratipakṣa*). Thus, it is established that from the perspective of ultimate truth (*siddhasādhyataḥ*), those two do not exist; however, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtyāt*), they do exist for the Blessed One. This is the intended meaning. // 7 //

Precisely because they have the nature of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is in reality no decrease or increase even for the perfections (*pāramitā*); thus he says, "And those which... and so forth. By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that it is not only the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), but rather these five perfections of the Victors, beginning with generosity (*dāna*) and so on, which are proclaimed to have the nature of distinguished phenomena (*viśiṣṭadharma*). Because they are like an illusion (*māyopama*), they are mere names; yet, one dedicates them toward unsurpassed enlightenment through conventional practice.

The Bodhisattva who, because he does not exalt himself, does not become conceited, does not fall away from his realizations; for this very reason, through the arising of the thought that illuminates the distinguished goal, he touches the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha. // 8 //
The eighteenth chapter, on Emptiness, in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthāvyākhyā*.
The nineteenth chapter, "The Chapter on Gaṅgadevā’s Sister.

[The author] speaks, beginning with "Of oil," etc., in order to refute—by means of an example—the objection that because the preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness are connected to one another through destruction and arising respectively without any continuity, how can there be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through the production of a consciousness that manifests a specific object, even from a conventional standpoint? [The example is as follows: When a wick is ignited by a lamp, at the moment of the first contact, the two flames possess a moment of merging; this is because they are indistinguishable in their simultaneous, combined arising, occurring without any interval between the second moment.

Since the relationship between the fuel and the burner—characterized by the nature of cause and effect—is untenable, the wick is not burned even by the subsequent moment of the lamp; for without the first moment, the arising of the subsequent moment is impossible, and thus that wick is not burned by what is non-existent. Nor is the wick burned by the flame upon its final impact, because apart from the first moment, there would follow the absurdity of eternal existence and so forth, and since conventional origination is absent, the relationship between fuel and burner—characterized by the nature of cause and effect—is untenable for that which is non-existent.

Because of the final impact of the flame, the first moment lacks the capacity to burn without the final moment; thus, the wick is not burned by the lamp existing at the first moment alone. In this way, since each [moment] individually lacks the capacity, it is through the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*)—by depending upon the moment of the lamp-wick produced from the initial conjunction—that the second moment of the lamp becomes distinct, having acquired a superior capacity through the causal relationship established conventionally (*saṃvṛti*).

The point is this: even if destruction were causeless, since the relationship of the burned and the burner—characterized as the relation between effect and cause—still exists, it would effectively be stated that the wick is burned by both the initial and the final moments. // 1 //

Applying the aforementioned meaning to the subject at hand, he says: "From the very first," and so forth. Thus, by touching upon the very first mind—which, because it does not manifest any objects that bring about the enlightenment of a Buddha—does not [attain] supreme enlightenment here in this teaching.

Furthermore, because that first moment of mind which touches awakening is non-existent in every respect and thus unreal, it cannot be realized by a second moment of mind, since there is no imparting of any further excellence or distinction; nor does the final mind alone attain the auspicious awakening through the pacification of all calamities, just as in the previous case, because that second moment of mind which attains awakening is non-existent in every respect.

Furthermore, it cannot be attained by the first mind alone because there is no production of a distinguished excellence. Therefore, it must be said that awakening is attained through both preceding and succeeding moments of mind, like the burning of a wick. // 2 //

Having generally indicated that both preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness are causes for awakening, [the author] now clarifies, by means of examples and through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that the first moment of consciousness is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). He says "seed," etc.: because of the contradiction between a permanent entity and causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—whether successively or simultaneously—a seed of the *aśvattha* tree or the like is momentary; and through a transformation in each successive moment, the branches and so forth, which produce the effect, come together as they properly attain their own nature.

Furthermore, that seed, having ceased at the time of the tree's production, would not exist at all initially; and if it were non-existent at first, there could be no *aśvattha* tree or the like. In the very same way, the mind is the primary cause and the fundamental basis regarding the object of enlightenment; from that very [mind], through the process of successive transformation, Buddhahood is attained. That [Buddhahood], having ceased at the time of its production, would not exist at all initially; and if it were non-existent at first, there could be no enlightenment. // 3 //

Clarifying that even the second moment of consciousness possesses causality, he says: "The seed," and so forth. By the power of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharmatā*), depending precisely upon the seed of barley, rice, or the like existing in the second and subsequent moments, that respective fruit—barley, rice, and so on—comes to be. And yet, that seed does not exist at the time of the fruit's production; for, since it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), it is nonetheless impossible to conclude that the continuity of moments does not exist in any way whatsoever, because a fruit arises that conforms to it.

In the same way, the second and subsequent moments of mind arise in dependence upon the power of the first moment of mind. This awakening of the Victors is, in reality, devoid of the intrinsic nature of existence, because it is impossible to perceive a causal relationship [between moments]; thus, the world here exists like an illusion. (4)

Having thus explained in detail, he concludes by saying "dakā" and so forth: Just as a jar is filled drop by drop with water—first by the initial falling of water and then gradually by subsequent drops—in the same way, through the mind, beginning with the first moment of mind directed toward unsurpassed enlightenment, [the Buddhas] become full. This is because, through the sequence of moments of mind starting from the second, they possess the nature of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and so on; and because they have attained the fulfillment of the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*) through white virtues (*śuklaguṇa*), they become full Buddhas. // 5 //

Having explained in detail what follows from the context, [the author] says "empty," etc., in order to state the characteristics of the irreversible Bodhisattva abiding in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Just as a boatman, being highly trained and skillful, travels about; because he is free from affliction, he goes to the further shore and returns from it by means of taking hold of the oar, and thus he does not stand at either bank, for that would be a place of falling into ruin, nor does he remain stationary.

In this ocean, because of the profundity of its arising and so forth, the Bodhisattva—understanding all phenomena as being, respectively, empty, signless, and wishless due to the absence of cause, effect, and intrinsic nature—does not touch cessation for the sake of turning away from reliance; yet, because he is governed by compassion and because there is still fear, he does not become one who courses in signs. Thus the meaning of the verse is to be applied. // 6 //

By means of explaining the characteristics of the non-retrogressive [bodhisattva], the Saṃgha of Bodhisattvas in training (śaikṣa) has been described; through the abandonment of conceptualizations regarding the defilement and purification of that [Saṃgha], one becomes one beyond training (aśaikṣa) due to the realization of the equality of both, as there is nothing further to be learned. Therefore, in order to illuminate the characteristics of the Saṃgha of those beyond training, he says "In this way," and so forth, for the sake of the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

By attaining the characteristics of irreversibility just described, the Bodhisattva, practicing through the cultivation of the equality of *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*, does not conceive the thought, "I have been prophesied by the Blessed Ones endowed with the ten powers; I shall attain enlightenment," because he has abandoned the conceptualization of purification. Furthermore, there should be no fear regarding the sign of enlightenment.

Because he has abandoned the conceptualization of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), and because all phenomena are unproduced, there is no substantial entity whatsoever here in this state of being like an illusion. Practicing in this manner, he courses in the wisdom of the Sugatas. (7)

Upon awakening to the equality of both, having cultivated that equality of both, one becomes a Buddha in one's own buddha-field. Immediately following this, in order to explain the purification of the two kinds of buddha-fields by way of the distinction between the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world, he says "in a wilderness," and so forth. This is an illustration [of various hardships], including waterless wildernesses, famine-stricken wildernesses, and worlds afflicted by disease.
Having seen other such places of misconduct within the worlds of sentient beings and their receptacles, [the Bodhisattva reflects]: "How should I purify the two kinds of buddha-fields?"

Because of the absence of such conceptual construction, there is no fear for Bodhisattvas, just as in the case of the sister Gaṅgadevā; rather, for the sake of purifying the two kinds of Buddha-fields in the future, they remain constantly engaged until the very limit of the future, never ceasing their efforts. Through their thorough knowledge of the means regarding the Mother [Prajñāpāramitā], they understand it clearly and do not give rise to even an atom of weariness in their minds. // 8 //
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Sister Gaṅgadevā," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthāvyākhyā* (Commentary on the Verses on the Accumulation of Precious Qualities).
The twentieth chapter, "Investigation of Skill in Means" (*Upāyakauśalyamīmāṃsāparivarta*).

Having accomplished the purification of the Buddha-field through skill in means, one must act for the sake of the Buddha’s work within one's own Buddha-field throughout saṃsāra according to the capacity of beings; thus, skill in means must be explained. In this regard, first describing its domain, he says: "Furthermore," and so forth. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva, while practicing in the wisdom of the Victors, by reason of non-arising, knows these aggregates—form and the rest—through the power of cultivation.

Since one does not realize [the truth] because it is empty from the very beginning, it should be explained that emptiness and so forth, which are like an illusion, constitute the domain of skill in means (*upāyakauśala*). To provide a response to the question of how one might fail to realize it even through practice, he speaks of "not being equal" (*asameti*) and so forth, thereby indicating the application of skill in means.

Although he does not perceive the existence of the reality of dharmas as previously described, he nevertheless beholds the realms of sentient beings with perfectly balanced compassion—arising from the knowledge of the means for accomplishing the welfare of the world—and with the desire to remove their suffering. Thus, by abiding in the interval between compassion and wisdom, he does not fall away from the qualities of a Buddha, such as the eighteen unique attributes (*āveṇika-dharma*), due to his capacity for application at the proper and improper times for realization; this is what is meant by "application" (*prayoga*). // 1 //

In this regard, first explaining by means of an illustration the method for transcending obstructive factors (*antarāyika-dharma*), he says: "Just as a man," and so forth. For example, a certain man, due to his proficiency in worldly affairs, is endowed with all virtues because he is adorned with qualities such as skill and heroism. He is powerful through his physical endowment of strength; he is invincible because he cannot be overcome by others; and he is well-prepared because of his thorough mastery of all characteristics.

Because he has practiced the physical transformations and other means for winning over others, he is skilled in the rules of the arts; because he is well-trained in archery and so forth, he has reached the perfection of weapons; because he has executed the prescribed methods in painting and other crafts, he is endowed with extensive artistic skill; because he is not one-sided toward wicked people, he is supreme in knowing the methods of illusion and the like; and because he is devoted to protecting virtuous people, he desires the welfare of the world.

Even one in such a situation, having been seized by someone—such as an enemy or the like—along with his mother and father, and having set out upon a path in the wilderness with his own wife, children, and others in a state of fear, might, due to the abundance of enemies, [be saved] by that very person who knows the methods of illusion. Having conjured many men who are fearless of life, heroic in their disposition to overcome adversaries, and who have emerged safely from the forest by transcending all obstacles, he proceeds in safety to his own place, namely, home.

He approaches [the goal]. In the same way, at whatever time a wise Bodhisattva, through the attainment of the manifestation of objectless loving-kindness (*anālambana-maitrī*), should—by bringing all sentient beings before him—bind and connect a great continuity of mind that desires their union with happiness within the realm of sentient beings; at that time, having transcended the four Māras, such as the sons of gods, and the two stages of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha, he stands at the forefront in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) because it carries one toward Buddhahood, yet he does not yet attain awakening because his task is not yet completed. (2–4)

Explaining the means for abiding in the established state by means of an illustration, he says: "In the spaces," and so forth. Just as, according to the sequence of the world's formation, the mass of water rests upon space together with the wind, and this great golden earth rests upon that [water], and the world-system of four continents rests upon that [earth]; therefore, in this regard, one should see that the primary cause for the enjoyment of sentient beings is precisely their karma.

Otherwise, how could space—which is characterized by the absence of all description—be the locus for the wind-mandala and so forth, since it is non-existent? Indeed, it could not be. And yet, that it is their locus is well-known in the scriptures (*pravacana*). Therefore, by reflecting upon this meaning through the forceful production of certainty regarding the aforementioned cause and effect—one should contemplate that the Bodhisattva, established in emptiness by means of the yoga of non-abiding, performs manifold activities for the sake of the world, because space is indeed another element (*dhātvantara*).

He displays various activities through clouds of emanations, which are infinite in each of their respective types. Because it is caused solely by that, his knowledge of the capacity of sentient beings according to their suitability and his knowledge of his own vows are merely sustained by that; due to the power of the aforementioned means, he does not attain final extinction (*nirvṛti*), yet because he has transcended the characteristics of substantial entities, he does not abide in emptiness. Such is the meaning: "and yet he remains therein. (5–6)

Explaining the means for following one’s former vows, he says: "In which [time]," and so forth. At the very time when the wise and learned bodhisattva cultivates this supreme emptiness—the non-apprehension of all phenomena—at that same time, because it pacifies all distractions, he should cultivate the Śūraṅgama and other samādhis as well as tranquility.

Thus, for a bodhisattva abiding between the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*), by the power of emptiness, he should not manifest signs (*nimitta*); nor should he, by the power of concentration, remain fixed in the signless (*animitta*). Therefore, through the efficacy of the aforementioned means, because there is no falling into either state as long as he so desires, he may—according to the sequence—be one who courses in the signless, whether in the "calm" [state] that leads to the attainment of *nirvāṇa* by grasping it, or in the "thoroughly calm" [state] by uprooting attachment to the signs of *saṃsāra*.

In order to explain the uncommon means, he says "of the bird," and so forth. Just as the track of two birds flying in the sky does not exist in the form of a reflection because it lacks a foundation, nor does it have a material form; and yet, due to the power of its two wings, the bird situated in that sky does not fall to the ground—so too the Bodhisattva, while practicing through the doors of the liberation of emptiness, does not touch nirvana because his mind is intent upon accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.

Since apprehension is to be abandoned, and one should not engage with signs, this method (upāya) taught for Bodhisattvas would be shown to be uncommon [to them] compared to that of the Śrāvakas and others. // 8 //

Explaining the method of non-attachment by means of an illustration, he says: "In archery," and so forth. Just as a certain man well-trained in the art of the bow, having properly shot an arrow upward, would not allow that first arrow to come to rest until, through a succession of other arrows, it falls to the ground of its own accord; [if he were to stop,] the arrow would fall while the man was still looking on.

In the very same way, the sons of the Victors, while practicing in this supreme perfection of wisdom whose nature is great skillful means, and while investigating through cultivation wisdom, compassion, and the rest, do not attain that supreme emptiness by the power of unassailable means until they have become fully perfected by their roots of virtue. (9–10)

In order to explain the means of emptiness as before, he says: "Just as a monk," and so forth. Because his afflictions have been destroyed, a monk—being endowed with the power of supreme supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) through the strength of the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*)—stands in the sky and performs a twin miracle (*yamaka-prātihārya*) for the sake of those to be trained by simultaneously displaying two wonders. That is to say, he demonstrates standing and walking, as well as lying down and sitting; and because these are well-practiced, he does not turn back.
Because he has cultivated the gateway to liberation that is emptiness, he does not become weary; the ellipsis "as long as he remains there" is to be supplied. // 11 //

In the very same way, the wise Bodhisattva, established in emptiness, having attained the excellence of knowledge and reached the perfection of the power of knowledge, wanders without a fixed abode because he is free from grasping at specific locations. Through the performance of manifold activities, he displays various deeds in the world out of compassion by means of clouds of emanations. Because each type [of emanation] is so abundant, they are infinite; because his emanations are well-practiced, he does not turn back, and by the power of emptiness and skillful means, he does not grow weary even for millions of eons. // 12 //

Explaining the method of signlessness (*animitta-upāya*) in the same way, he says: "Just as a man," and so forth. Just as some man, standing on the edge of a great precipice, takes up two umbrellas with both hands and gazes [upward], because it is not the proper time, [he encounters] untimely wind; then, having cast himself down into the great precipice, he does not cause himself to fall into a rugged abyss or produce suffering, until he reaches his intended destination there.

Abiding thus in compassion, the wise Bodhisattva, embraced by the two parasols of wisdom and skillful means, investigates phenomena through the analytical discernment of the certainty of the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; yet, by the power of the means of signlessness, he does not touch upon extinction, but rather demonstrates it. (13–14)

And likewise, through teaching, he informs others of the dharmas by means of the method of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) preceded by examples, saying "Like a jewel," and so forth: Just as a man seeking jewels, having gone to an island of jewels because it is a source of lapis lazuli and other gems, might live there happily; yet even though he is the caravan leader, upon obtaining the jewels, he would return home again.

Because one is bound by affection, when one is afflicted by poverty and the like, the thought "the assembly of beings" arises in the mind through its being brought to presence; thus, the connection should be understood as distributed [between the two clauses]. In exactly the same way, having entered into emptiness, a person—because he is a mine of the jewels of virtue—and though the Bodhisattva, finding no island of refuge among the powers of meditation, the faculties, and so forth, might touch upon nirvāṇa with delight, nevertheless, by the power of his former vows, all sentient beings who suffer from birth and other afflictions remain present in his mind.
Therefore, because of the power of the method of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), one should not actualize cessation (*nirvṛti*) by bringing it face-to-face; this is the intended meaning. // 15–16 //

In order to state the means for the signs of irreversibility (*avaivartika-liṅga*) in exactly that same way, he says: "Or within," and so forth. "Within" refers to a village, market town, city, or the like; just as a merchant might go there for a desired purpose in order to fully understand the prices for buying and selling. Therefore, he does not remain there in that city or elsewhere with a fixed mind, nor even on the island of jewels; rather, because he understands the means of escaping from thieves and the like, he is skilled in the path and wise because of his capacity to acquire wealth through superior discourse.

Furthermore, because he has taken up compassion for sentient beings within the household and does not depart from it, the wise and learned Bodhisattva—through the union of compassion and wisdom—becomes skilled in practice regarding the liberation of both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas in all respects, for the sake of those beings to be trained by him. Because he does not abandon the welfare of sentient beings, he does not remain fixed in the direct realization [of cessation].

Because they have not yet fulfilled all that was to be done, they likewise do not abide in the Tathāgata’s gnosis; and because they have understood the defects of the conditioned, they do not abide in the conditioned. For this very reason, by thoroughly knowing the qualities and defects respectively on the universal path, the wise one becomes one who knows the method; thus, this should be declared as the uncommon dharma of those who are irreversible. (17–18)

To explain the meaning of the immeasurable means (*apramāṇopāya*), he says "At which time" (*yaṃ kāli*) and so forth. At whatever time one has cultivated loving-kindness (*maitrī*)—which takes the form of a desire for union with happiness—toward all beings in the world, and then meditates upon the concentrations (*samādhi*) of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), at that time, by the power of having emptiness and so forth as the objects of focus for immeasurable sentient beings, it is impossible [for him to fall back]; for whether this son of the Conqueror attains nirvāṇa, or even if he remains in the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), he can no longer be designated [as falling back]. This is the meaning of the verse. (19)

Clarifying this very point, he says "Just as," and so forth. Just as a conjured person (*nirmita-puruṣa*)—because he has come within the range of vision of those whose eyes are afflicted by mantras and the like—is not invisible by way of logic due to the absence of [independent] investigation, it should be connected [to the question]: whether or not he can be designated again by that name.

Likewise, a bodhisattva, practicing preceded by the objective support of sentient beings, [investigates] whether it is possible or not to designate again by name—within the realm of the conditioned or the unconditioned—the gateway to the doors of liberation such as emptiness; this is the connection with what precedes. Thus, having indicated each subsequent means as the cause for each preceding means, the tenfold means is presented according to its predominance and its distinctions—as in the *Śatasāhasrikā*—because all other means are included within it. // 20 //

Concluding that no further reason need be stated, he says: "If questioned," and so forth. When a bodhisattva, being questioned by the sons of the Conquerors (*jinaputra*), does not provide an explanation—due to his having practiced the conduct [of the bodhisattvas], because of the detailed exposition of the various conducts, the faculties, and the profound dharmas, and because of his lack of thorough knowledge regarding the aforementioned means—this is due to the liberations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Furthermore, because he does not indicate the dharmas of the stage of non-retrogression through a brief explanation of the arising of the thought that does not abandon any sentient being, it is said that he should be known as one who has not yet received a prophecy; thus is the realization of all aspects (sarvākārābhisambodha) described. And so it has been said:

"The aspects, along with their applications, the virtues and faults with their characteristics, the stages conducive to liberation and penetration, and the group of those in training and those who are non-retrogressive."
The equality of existence and peace, the supreme purification of the field, and the realization of all aspects—this is [the path] together with skill in means. (21)

Now, regarding the "Culminating Clear Realization" (*mūrdhābhisamaya*), which is the ultimate limit of excellence for one who has attained the complete awakening in all its aspects, the author speaks first of its signs, beginning with the words "Arhat... and so forth: "He who does not long for the stage of an Arhat, the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, or the triple world; who, through the practice of the Truths, sees the Buddhas even in his dreams and teaches the Dharma to the world—he should be known as one who has been prophesied as irreversible from the Culminating Clear Realization."

Likewise, having perceived through a dream those beings who have fallen into the three miserable realms (*apāya*), he makes this vow: "At that very moment, may I dry up the miserable realms. Furthermore, even while in the state of dreaming, he pacifies masses of fire in cities and other places by means of the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*). One should know that such a person is irreversible (*avaivartika*) and thus prophesied (*vyākṛta*). Likewise, in the world of humans, he pacifies various afflictions caused by spirits and demons through the empowerment of truth.

Out of a mind intent on favoring the world, he is compassionate for their welfare; yet, because he does not foster self-exaltation through such things as the departure of spirits or demons, he does not give rise to conceit (*māna*). Nor is he one who disparages others, thinking, "Just as before, this [bodhisattva] too is irreversible and has received his prediction. This should be understood. (22–24)
The twentieth chapter, "Investigation of Skill in Means," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*.
The twenty-first chapter, "On the Deeds of Māra.

Because one might depart due to the influence of Māra, [the author] says, "This is not a sign," beginning with "Then... and so forth: "Then, if pride arises in this Bodhisattva, thinking, 'I have been prophesied, since my various acts of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*) have been successful,' and if he thus despises another Bodhisattva who has received a prophecy because of such contempt, then it should be known that this Bodhisattva stands in pride; because he exalts himself merely by that much due to being influenced by Māra, he is one whose mind is deficient in wisdom. (1)

In this context, while indicating the various classifications of the deeds of Māra (*mārakarman*), he speaks of the meaning of the deeds of Māra by way of names, beginning with the word "name" (*nāma*). Because of the designations of names given by one's mother and others, Māra will approach by means of the basis of names and speak as follows: "This is your name; or that of your mother and father, or even up to the seventh person in the lineage who has come down to you—this is his name," he will say.

"In this way, when you become a Buddha, even then this very name that was conceived by that mind shall be exactly so," he will say. Having heard that, whoever gives rise to pride should be known as one whose intellect is small and who is possessed by Māra; this is the connection with what is to be said next. // 2 //

Regarding the purpose of the deeds of Māra by way of the ascetic qualities (*dhūtaguṇa*), he says "the ascetic" and so forth. He will say: "By means of such ascetic qualities as being a mendicant for alms-food (*paiṇḍapātika*) and so on, that yogin will become endowed with them; even previously, you must have possessed such qualities. And the Bodhisattva who, having heard this, gives rise to conceit (*abhimāna*), should be known as one from whom Māra has taken possession through a false attribution (*māropasthāna*); that is to say, he is one of little intelligence and inferior intention. // 3 //

He speaks of the work of Māra even by way of dwelling in seclusion, beginning with the words "secluded," and so forth. Because they are devoid of people, the villages and towns are "secluded. Because they are possessed of flowing water and the like, they are "mountain caves. Because one stays at a distance of only one *krośa* from the village after having abandoned it, they are "wildernesses" (*araṇya*).

If, while frequenting forest retreats that are secluded because they are free from tigers and other such dangers, a bodhisattva exalts himself out of pride in his virtues and so forth, and disparages others by pointing out their deformities, then he should be known as one whose Māra has arisen; he is of little intelligence and possesses an unwholesome disposition. Thus it is said. (4)

How, then, is there dwelling in solitude? To this he says: "In a village," and so forth. While wandering in villages such as Vaideha, in regions such as Campā, in kingdoms, and in towns such as Pāṭaliputra, they never generate a longing for Arhatship or Pratyekabuddhahood therein. Rather, because they are engaged in the maturation of sentient beings to be trained—such as Śrāvakas—and because they have set out toward unsurpassed enlightenment with a correct intention, they dwell endowed with awakening. This is what was just mentioned. It is called "solitude" (viveka) because it involves being separated from all that is unwholesome.
Because they are born from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) which possesses the aforementioned related qualities, [they are] the sons of the Sugata. // 5 //

But another [kind of person] does not possess discernment at all; thus he says, "He who... and so forth. A bodhisattva who might dwell for many millions of years in mountain caves five hundred yojanas in extent—places crowded with fierce creatures, beasts of prey, and snakes—and yet does not know this discernment just described because he is possessed of the mental orientations of the śrāvakas and others, would dwell in confusion. Having failed to attain the state of a bodhisattva, he is one who has attained pride through the conceit of being a bodhisattva. // 6 //

And he says "so ca" and so forth, meaning that this very person has not transcended the domain of ordinary men (*mānava*). If that bodhisattva, out of delusion regarding the welfare of the world, looks down upon other bodhisattvas who are engaged [in practice], as well as those who have attained the powers such as faith whose nature consists of the stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) which are the form of the attainments (*samāpatti*), the faculties (*indriya*) such as faith whose nature consists of the levels of heat (*ūṣman*) and summits (*mūrdhan*), the heroic strides (*śūraṅgama*), and the liberations (*vimokṣa*) such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
"He does not disparage them by saying, 'These are Bodhisattvas who dwell in the seclusion of the forest'; rather, he is told by the Victor: 'This one stands within the domain of Māra. // 7 //

Having explained this in detail, he concludes by saying "in the vicinity of a village," and so forth. One who dwells either in the vicinity of a village or in the forest—being entirely free from the desire for the state of a Śrāvaka and so on, being devoid of the minds of the two vehicles, and being fixed exclusively upon unsurpassed enlightenment—is one whose supreme enlightenment is certain; such a Bodhisattva weighs other forms of seclusion associated with the Śrāvakas and others as bringing about only limited qualities. For this very reason, because it causes [those qualities] to perish, he "wears them away" (kṣiṇoti).
For this aforementioned solitude belongs to the sons of the Conquerors who have set out for the sake of the world. // 8 //
The twenty-first chapter, on the Deeds of Māra, in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*.
The Twenty-second Chapter: On the Spiritual Friend.

Because this very fault arises from a lack of full understanding, its antidote must be cultivated; thus he says, "Therefore," and so forth. Since the aforementioned fault results from overweening pride (*abhimāna*), the wise person—having utterly destroyed that pride by avoiding the means for falling into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)—should, with great conviction and a mind heavy with resolve, seek supreme enlightenment. Like a patient seeking a physician to cure the chronic diseases of passion and the like, one should attend upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) with devotion and without laziness. (1)

Furthermore, as to who the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are, he says "the Buddha," and so forth. The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas set out for supreme enlightenment are the spiritual friends; and these six perfections (pāramitā) have been taught [as such]. Since those [Buddhas and others] are instructors who, by means of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, provide guidance, and since these perfections beginning with generosity constitute the ground of practice (*pratipattibhūmi*) because they are being performed, one awakens to the enlightenment of a Buddha through these two causes. Therefore, the intended meaning is that the spiritual friend is not something separate from [that enlightenment]. // 2 //

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the *pāramitās* alone do not constitute the ground of practice? How, then, is this [claim] logical? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Transcended," and so forth. Those Blessed Buddhas who have transcended by virtue of being past, who have arrived by virtue of being in the future, and who abide by virtue of being present throughout the ten directions—for all of them, this path characterized by the *pāramitās* is the means to attain Buddhahood; because it is non-dual, it is not otherwise, for otherwise there would be no abandonment of error.

Because they dispel the darkness of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they are an illumination; because they remove the gloom of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they are a torch. Likewise, for those bodhisattvas who have set out for supreme enlightenment, they are of the nature of light because they produce the light of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Furthermore, through their relinquishment and production, and by way of instruction, they become like teachers on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Therefore, since these perfections (*pāramitā*) have been correctly taught, the intended meaning is that this alone is the stage of practice (*pratipattibhūmi*). // 3 //

Having concluded what arose incidentally, [the author] now states "Just as wisdom," and so forth, in order to show that one should not form an attachment even to the aforementioned sign (*liṅga*) in the context at hand: "Just as one understands the Perfection of Wisdom to be empty—characterized by being devoid of a nature of oneness or manyness like an illusion—so too does one understand all these phenomena, characterized by form and so forth, to be empty.

Therefore, for one who understands all phenomena through this characteristic of emptiness, if they practice according to the aforementioned sign, then practicing in this way, they practice in the wisdom of the Sugatas. // 4 //

If it is asked how the distinction between affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) is established given that all phenomena (*dharma*), whose characteristics are as previously described, are empty, he says: "By food," and so forth. Through their attachment to a self and what belongs to a self, sentient beings conceptualize foods such as edible morsels and sensual pleasures such as forms and so on. With minds distressed by the suffering of acquiring, guarding, losing, and grieving over these, they constantly transmigrate through taking up birth due to their perverted intellects.

In reality, however, these two—the notion of "I" and the notion that "this is mine"—are both empty because they are unproduced, despite being experienced as such. Therefore, through the force of one's own misconceptions regarding space, this knot of the self is tied by people who, due to their lack of skill in conventional discourse, find it difficult to untie, like fools. This is the sense in which the state of affliction is established. // 5 //

If one asks, "In what way is the establishment of affliction [saṃkleśa] due to the power of one's own cognitive distortions (viparyāsa)? he says: "Just as," and so forth. Just as a person who, out of a suspicion regarding poison and a distortion concerning poison, perceives poison and accepts it as such, is afflicted by that very poison—even though the poison has not entered his stomach because it does not exist [therein]—so too, because the Noble Path has not arisen, the fool, through the power of cognitive distortion, appropriates [the notion]: "I" and "this is my dharma. When there is a self, there arises the conception of "other"; from the division of self and other, there arise grasping and aversion.
All defects arise when these two are conjoined.

Thus, at the very moment the notion of a self arises, because of the emptiness resulting from the discernment of superimposed phenomena, the fool is [realized to be] non-existent; by implication, through the reversal of what was previously stated, the establishment of purification occurs—this is the intended meaning. // 6 //

Concluding the establishment of both [truths] by relying upon the two truths, he says "Just as... and so forth. Just as grasping and adherence are conventionally manifested, so too are affliction and purification described.
