However, regarding the statement "I" and "my dharma," just as these are not perceived through adherence, so they do not exist in reality; for since there is no delusion in this state of being like an illusion, no one is afflicted or purified, because there is no removal of bondage. The remainder of the sense is that the Bodhisattva realizes the reality of phenomena through the perfection of wisdom. // 7 //

Since the increase of the *mūrdhābhisamaya* (culminating clear realization) characterized by such a mark must be explained, he says "as many as... and so forth: Suppose all sentient beings dwelling here in Jambūdvīpa were to each generate the mind for supreme enlightenment and give gifts to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others for many thousands of millions of years, and they were all to further dedicate those merits toward enlightenment, which is the cause for the fulfillment of the goals desired by the world.

And if another single person, engaged in the supreme perfection through the wisdom of the nature of the culminating realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*), were to correctly practice it for even a single day—at least in this regard, because of being endowed with the increase of every kind of application to the practice of the perfection of wisdom—the aforementioned mass of giving by those beings does not become even a fraction of a cause for merit when compared to the merit of that [other] person. Therefore, the remainder [of the meaning] is that the perfection of wisdom should always be followed with untiring cultivation. (8–9)

This mother alone is not to be practiced; rather, compassion must also be cultivated. Thus he says, "Moving," and so forth: When the son of the Conqueror, the yogi, moving within the supreme perfection of wisdom whose intrinsic nature has been described, generates great compassion through the state of having bestowed his concentration upon it, and does not harbor the notion of a "sentient being" due to an adherence to the existence of things, then he becomes a wise man in the entire world, acting with prior reflection.
Because they are fields of merit and thus worthy of offerings, he enjoys sense objects and alms-food without fail, in view of their capacity to necessarily yield fruit at all times. (10)

Therefore, one must apply oneself to compassion for the sake of sentient beings and to wisdom; thus he says "for a long time," and so forth. That Bodhisattva who here rightly desires to liberate for a long duration those bound by the power of error regarding their own objects—the gods, humans, and the beings in the three lower realms such as the hells—and who desires to show the vast path of the Mahāyāna, the shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, to the realm of sentient beings; he should be joined day and night with the perfection of wisdom accompanied by compassion. (11)

Clarifying this very point by means of an illustration, he says: "Just as a man," and so forth. For example, suppose a certain man, because of its excellence, were to obtain a preeminent jewel that he had previously possessed; having obtained it again at a later time, he would become joyful. Yet, immediately after his joy, having obtained it, he might lose it due to the recurrence of distractions and the like, and thus fail to attain composure once more.

Therefore, by constantly bringing to mind the separation from the desired object known as "non-separation" (*avinābhāva*), one should become yearning for the jewels. In the very same way, by one who has set out for supreme enlightenment, mental attention toward the perfection of wisdom—which is like a jewel because it is difficult to find and is accompanied by compassion—must not be abandoned.

Therefore, just as one might wrap a jewel in cloth or similar materials, a Bodhisattva who possesses an undestroyed jewel-like nature should grasp the *Prajñāpāramitā* and, through long-term practice, maintain a continuous connection with it. When he does so, because he has entered the correct path, he will swiftly attain Nirvāṇa. (12–13)
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Spiritual Friend."
The twenty-third chapter, the *Śakraparivarta*.

Having generally described the fruit resulting from the increase of both compassion and wisdom, the author now speaks—beginning with the words "Just as at its rising," etc.—to specifically demonstrate the overcoming of opposing factors by means of an illustration:

Just as the sun, upon its rising, reaches its zenith and, free from clouds, dispels the mass of all darkness and overcomes it with its garlands of rays, so too does it surpass all living beings such as tiny fireflies by its own radiance, as well as all the hosts of stars headed by Venus and Jupiter, and even the light of the moon itself.

Thus, practicing in wisdom—the supreme perfection whose nature consists of the meaning as previously described—the wise Bodhisattva, having shaken off the entire mass of views such as the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is a thicket because it is the cause for the arising of all [unwholesome] objects, surpasses all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas in the world. By practicing the signless (*animitta*) and empty (*śūnya*) through the ultimate increase of the aforementioned compassion and wisdom, the Bodhisattva becomes "great" by virtue of the greatness of his abandonment; such is the intended meaning. (1–2)

Having thus explained the overcoming of the opposing factors (*vipakṣa*), he now says "Just as... and so forth, in order to speak of the attainment of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) in the same manner. Just as a prince, because of his habit of sharing with his servants, is a giver of wealth; because of his skill in acquiring resources by following the path of policy, he is one who desires wealth; because he is to be accepted as the preeminent leader among all princes, he is the best; and because he is served by the entire world, he is approachable.

Since he now gladdens sentient beings with honors and the like even while in this state devoid of consciousness, it follows that when he is firmly established in sovereignty by having received consecration, he—while bearing the cloth [painting]—will certainly not be one who gladdens sentient beings; such is the intended meaning.

Likewise, the wise Bodhisattva who practices wisdom conjoined with compassion possesses the power of realizing the antidotes; because he is one whose nature is to teach the Dharma and discourse on it, he becomes a provider of the vision of the deathless—the path of seeing and so forth—for gods and humans. For this very reason, even now, while in a state of limited realization, he is dedicated to the happiness of sentient beings by means of illuminating the path of seeing and the rest.

Therefore, it is all the more certain that as long as he remains—having abandoned all obscurations along with their latent tendencies—he will then be devoted to the happiness of sentient beings within the kingdom of Dharma; this is how it connects with what precedes. (3–4)
The twenty-third chapter, "Śakra," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthāvyākhyā*.
The twenty-fourth chapter, "On Arrogance.

Thus, when the antidote has increased to such an extent that Māra, having overstepped his own domain, becomes filled with anxiety, he says: "Māra also," and so forth. At the time when the antidote arises, Māra becomes "pierced by a thorn" because he experiences weak, middling, or intense dejection. For this very reason, he is afflicted by grief, suffering, and displeasure of mind, and thus he would become one of little strength.

In every direction and intermediate direction, he hurls torches for the sake of burning and to instill fear; yet, how could this [Māra] cause the Bodhisattva to become dejected in his cultivation of the counteractive measures? Even so, he is unable to create an obstacle. // 1 //

To whom [is he] powerless? He says: "When," and so forth. When they become wise, endowed with the perfection of compassion and a perfectly pure intention, and by the power of cultivation see the meaning of the supreme *prajñāpāramitā* both day and night—then, through the practice of compassion and wisdom, they are equal to birds that travel through the sky by means of body, mind (the latter being illustrative of speech as well), because they do not abide exclusively in any one place. Thus, by virtue of their equality, they have become like them.

How could he find an opportunity against them? Because Kṛṣṇa acts without assistance, even though he is a kinsman of Kṛṣṇa, the sense is that he will not succeed at all because [the enemies] are acting correctly. // 2 //

But it prevails over those who have set out upon an incorrect path; thus he says "quarreling," and so forth. When Bodhisattvas have fallen into quarreling due to the onset of verbal disputes in their own places, into contention through litigating before royal courts and the like, into opposition through the occurrence of mutual hatred and so on, and when they wander about with minds enraged by the arousal of anger—at that time, Māra becomes satisfied because he has gained an opportunity for entry; for this very reason, his supreme joy arises from the production of such pleasure.

Furthermore, because these two engage in quarrels and the like, they will be far removed from the Blessed One’s wisdom due to their reliance on such [conflict]; likewise, because they lack the means for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, they will be far removed from the qualities of a Buddha, being like *piśāca* demons; and because they have not desisted from the obstacles of quarreling and so forth, they will bring about the abandonment of their own vow.

And when, due to an abundance of hatred, there is no awakening for those who are wicked, who are intolerant of harming others and the like, and who lack patience, then Māra will be pleased because of his great retinue; and the army of Māra will likewise rejoice in unrighteousness, strife, and so forth—this is the intended meaning. (3–4)

If it is asked, "How then is the attainment of enlightenment [prevented]? he says: "He who [is a] bodhisattva," and so forth. The meaning is this: one who, having been predicted (vyākṛta), or—since this is an indication for those not yet predicted (avyākṛta)—having corrupted his mind by giving rise to hatred and the like toward one who is unpredicated, initiates a dispute and does not perform confession and so on.

Therefore, for as many moments of consciousness as are associated with faults such as hatred—which have become like barren wastelands through the impairment of the wholesome—one must don the armor again for the sake of removing the evil arising from strife and so forth over that many eons, and for the sake of attaining the antidote, provided that Buddhahood has not been abandoned; and it is the thought that enlightenment is attained in this manner. // 5 //

He speaks also for the sake of another method, beginning with "Then," and so forth: "Then, if a thought arises in the mind that [strife and the like] are unwholesome because they obstruct awakening—since Buddhas touch awakening through being endowed with the perfection of patience—one who, having reflected thus, confesses by means of the verse on the confession of sins, and further enters into a vow of restraint before someone else never to do it again in the future."

Because they cause [others] to gain conviction or because they approach that very person, he thus trains here in the Buddha-dharma as one who knows the correct path of the bodhisattva—up to this point. // 6 //
The twenty-fourth chapter, on Conceit, in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthāvyākhyā*.
The twenty-fifth chapter, "On Training.

Having first dispelled the pride of Māra, it is said—beginning with the words "He who," etc.—that the purification of training must be practiced in this way: that Bodhisattva who, while training for Buddhahood and so forth, does not approach [it] from the perspective of ultimate reality; who finds no training whatsoever in the form of an action, nor a self as a trainee in the form of an agent; and who likewise does not perceive the phenomena being trained in as objects of action—because of this very non-perception—he does not even perceive non-training or the phenomena that are not to be trained in.

Thus, one who trains conventionally—without conceptualizing the duality of training and non-training through the purity of the three spheres—trains here in the excellence of the dharmas such as the ten wholesome paths that bring about Buddhahood, by way of attaining the beneficial and abandoning the harmful; this is the intended meaning. // 1 //

And he alone, through the departure from all immorality (*dauḥśīlya*), is one who accomplishes the qualities of a Buddha; thus it says, "He who [is a Bodhisattva]," and so forth. That very Bodhisattva, because he does not transgress the two truths, understands this training (*śikṣā*) just described. Since he never fails to fulfill it through complete practice, he does not become immoral due to a deficiency in training; therefore, being one who accomplishes [the goal], he trains in the qualities of a Buddha. It is not otherwise, in this sequential manner, regarding the training based upon the non-duality of truth.
Being exceptionally skilled in training, he would become utterly free from objective apprehension due to the disappearance of the fault of falling into the perception of entities. // 2 //

He asks, "Why is this so? and replies with the words beginning "They train" (*śikṣante*). Just as when the rays of the sun itself moving through the sky spread across the intermediate space, darkness does not remain before it; in the same way, for the wise who are training in the aforementioned instruction—which relies upon both truths—their unwholesome [states] do not arise even for a single moment of mind, because they possess an abundance of the light of knowledge due to their being "light-makers" (*prabhākara*) whose qualities have arisen as described. This is the intended meaning. // 3 //

If it is asked: "Since training in other perfections such as generosity and so forth exists, why is training prescribed in the perfection of wisdom alone? he says: "Wisdom," and so forth. Because for the sons of the Conquerors who train in the perfection of wisdom alone, there is the application of awakening to all phenomena, they train with [all] the perfections as their retinue; therefore, all the remaining perfections are included here. Furthermore, regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it is as taught in the *Brahmajālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* concerning the sixty-two views.

Because they arise through its sovereignty, these perfections of giving and so forth, when practiced with the complete purity of the three spheres, become included within the perfection of wisdom. // 4 //

Having thus explained by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he also speaks by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), beginning with "Just as," and so forth: "Just as previously, when life-force (*jīvitendriya*) is being extinguished due to the cessation of the lifespan projected by a prior birth, whatever great collection of sense-faculties there may be—beginning with the eye faculty—all that becomes extinguished because of the absence of its basis (*āśraya*). In the same way, for the wise ones who have practiced in wisdom—the supreme beings who are Bodhisattvas—all the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity and the rest are encompassed through the aforementioned capacity."

When all of those [other perfections] are examined (or obstructed) within the perfection of wisdom, they become obstructed. Therefore, the sense is that training is prescribed in the perfection of wisdom alone. // 5 //

If it is argued that, in this way, because the training in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) gives rise to qualities such as those of a *śrāvaka* in every training, it is indeed a fault, he says: "And those who... and so forth. Even those qualities of a *śrāvaka*, such as their path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and so on, as well as all those of the *pratyekabuddhas*—in all of these, the wise Bodhisattva, having been trained with the intention of benefiting the sentient beings to be converted by them, does not abide therein, because he has been trained for the sake of another [the ultimate goal].

Likewise, he does not even long for the virtues of those such as the śrāvakas; therefore, thinking "one must train for the sake of others," he trains in this matter, and thus there is no fault because of this non-realization [of those lower goals]. // 6 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "Training."
The twenty-sixth chapter, "Like an Illusion.

Since it must be stated how the firm establishment of that which has thus increased through growth occurs, he says: "Of the irreversible one," and so forth. When a bodhisattva rejoices with a correct intention in the production of the thought [of awakening] by one who is irreversible and specifically set out for supreme awakening, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings through great compassion—at that time, the measure of Mount Sumeru in the trichiliocosm would have to be taken up and weighed on the tip of a single hair.

However, it is not possible to grasp the measure of that son of the Conqueror who has become established through rejoicing in virtue; the sense is that because this is merely an illustration, it is likewise impossible to grasp the measure of other established dharmas. // 1 //

Having thus established [the practice], it must be explained how the mind of one so established remains fixed; therefore, he says "as many as," and so forth: "As many beings as there are who, on the stages of equipment and so forth, seek the wholesome, and on the stages of Joy and so forth, desire liberation."

Whatever mass of merit is rejoiced in by all of them, because they have attained a state of mental abiding whose nature is a merit even greater than that, those bodhisattvas will gradually attain the qualities of a Victor for the sake of sentient beings and bestow the Dharma upon the world so that all suffering born of perversion may be removed. Furthermore, these characteristics and so forth should be understood as having the nature of the four stages conducive to penetration—Heat and the others—in their sequence within the *Mūrdhābhisamaya*. // 2 //

Immediately following the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) comes the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). In that context, there are four kinds of discordant factors (*vipakṣa*), namely the conceptualizations of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakavikalpa*). Since it must be stated that these are abandoned through the adoption of their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), [the author] first says "He who, regarding awakening... and so forth, in order to explain the first conceptualization of the grasped, which has as its basis the side of active involvement (*pravṛttipakṣa*).

The Bodhisattva who, in the stage of application to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prayogāvasthā*), having abandoned conceptualization as previously described, is non-conceptual; who thoroughly understands all phenomena as empty and signless because they are devoid of the nature of cause and effect; who, through the exclusion of all superimposed phenomena, perceives them as free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); and who, for that very reason, does not seek awakening by means of wisdom through the delineation of the aforementioned conceptualizations—such a one is a "Yogin" because he is connected by way of positive concomitance to the relationship of cause and effect, and because he is endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom consisting of the path of seeing, being joined with the mental attention of the path of seeing. (3)

The second [type of conceptualization], which has the entire side of cessation as its basis and is to be abandoned through the conceptualization of the apprehended object, is likewise stated by means of an example, beginning with "space" (*ākāśa*). Just as there would be no contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion between space and the sky, because that contradiction—though it might be reached in some place or in some manner—is not found between that element of space and that sky; rather, what [is the contradiction] in the case of sound, given its denotation of transience within its own nature?

The meaning is that there is no possibility of contradiction with its activity (*kāritra*). Likewise, the wise Bodhisattva who has practiced within wisdom, which has the nature of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), becomes like space due to the attainment of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñāna*); during the state of the functioning of the mind and mental factors of the path of seeing, he is one whose conduct is pacified because of the abandonment of the aforementioned conceptualizations. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no contradiction for him with anything whatsoever. // 4 //

Having thus indicated the two types of conceptualization regarding the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), the two types of conceptualization regarding the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) must now be explained. First, indicating that the conceptualizations of the subject based on a person existing as a substantial entity (*dravyasat*) are to be abandoned, he says "Just as... and so forth: Just as a person created by a magician does not have such a thought—because of its lack of conceptualization—as "I shall please this assembled audience."

And yet, that very conjured person performs an action due to the conceit of generating a cognition in which a specific object appears; for this very reason, spectators perceive him as displaying various actions through the power of their own conceit. However, because he is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, that conjured person has no body, nor mind, nor the essential nature of speech, nor even a name.

Likewise, when a Bodhisattva practices in wisdom during the stage of application for the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), there never arises in his mind the thought, "Having awakened, I shall liberate [beings] by means of awakening and the teaching of the Dharma to the world. Nevertheless, he displays various births among the realms of gods and others through manifold diversity, as well as various activities for the sake of sentient beings; because these are merely conventional and resemble an illusion, and because he is free from the aforementioned conceptual constructions, he moves without conceptualization. (5–6)

And in order to state, as before, that the second type of conceptualization of a grasper—which has a person existing as a mere designation (prajñaptisat-pudgala) as its basis—is to be abandoned, he says "just as" and so forth: Just as a Buddha’s magical creation performs the work of a Buddha because it has the nature of a specific emanation, yet no pride arises in it because it is non-conceptual; for one who performs some task, pride does not arise toward oneself due to the production of self-importance.

Likewise, when wisdom—which has as its intrinsic nature the activity of the mind and mental factors on the path of seeing—has abandoned conceptualization as previously described, the wise Bodhisattva who has practiced it demonstrates that all activity is, respectively, like a magical creation or an illusion, due to being devoid of the existence of cause and fruit. Thus, through the abandonment of the fourfold conceptualization by means of non-attachment, he becomes a performer of all purposeful activities. // 7 //

Concluding as before, he says "pala" and so forth: Just as a wooden automaton made by a skilled carpenter—such as Takṣaka—who is learned because he has been trained according to instruction, and who acts through his own ingenuity and wisdom, performs all its functions by producing an appearance similar to that of a man or a woman; so too [is the case here].

Likewise, the wise Bodhisattva who practices within wisdom—of the nature just described—by abandoning the fourfold conceptualization, performs all the activities of the world through a cognition that is free from attachment to subject and object, like a wish-fulfilling gem that is itself non-conceptual. // 8 //
The twenty-sixth chapter, "The Illusion-like," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthāvyākhyā*.
The twenty-seventh chapter, "The Chapter on Māra":

It is not only because of the non-deficiency in abandoning the four conceptualizations as described that [the practice] performs its purposeful activity and is praised by the Buddhas and others; thus he says, "In this way," and so forth. In this way, for the wise Bodhisattvas who practice by abandoning the four conceptualizations as described, the vast assemblies of gods headed by Śakra, with palms joined, bow their minds and pay homage through body and speech.
Even all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as many as exist throughout the world-systems in the ten directions, all of them proclaim the garland of praise for his virtues. // 1 //

For this very reason, he says "as many as... and so forth, [to show] that one would indeed transcend Māra. However many beings exist in as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, if all of them, by way of conceptual construction, were to become Māras; and if each one of them were further to manifest that same number of Māras from every single pore of their skin—even then, they would not be able to create an obstacle for the wise one. (2)

Having thus primarily explained the sequence of transcending the Māra of the sons of gods (*devaputramāra*), he speaks of the transcendence of the four Māras, saying "by four causes," and so forth. By the very abandonment of the four conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) as described, through the power of wisdom (*prajñā*), one becomes an abider in emptiness (*śūnyatā*); yet, by the efficacy of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one does not abandon sentient beings.

Because he fulfills the remaining aims that were promised, he acts according to his word through truth; and because he is endowed with the perfection of merit and knowledge, he becomes sustained by the Sugata. By these four causes, he is powerful due to the perfection of physical strength, wise because his speech is unimpeded, and difficult to overcome because his mind cannot be altered. Therefore, the meaning of the verse should be applied as follows: he cannot be shaken by the Māra of the aggregates and the other types of Māras. (3)

Now, explaining the reason why the path of seeing (darśanamārga), when accompanied by this [practice], is considered the bringer of great awakening (mahābodhi), he says: "The bodhisattva who," and so forth. That bodhisattva, for the sake of establishing others through the demonstration of the path of seeing and so forth regarding great awakening, and for the very purpose of the sign of awakening, likewise resolves with his mind through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) upon this Mother Prajñāpāramitā—the mother of the Tathāgatas—for the sake of correctly returning [the teaching] by way of the text, meaning, and so on. He speaks while resolving thus.

And because one personally performs such acts as writing [the scriptures] for the sake of attaining awakening, one is engaged with direct practice; and because one applies oneself to the means for omniscience with a correct intention, one should be known as having set out [on the path]. // 4 //

Demonstrating through an example that only the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), when accompanied by the causes as previously specified, possesses the capacity for the non-appearance of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), he says "And not... and so forth. Just as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)—which is the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*) because its intrinsic nature is suchness (*tathatā*)—does not attain the status of being a location, or rather, does not abide in a location; for in the atmosphere of the sky, which is characterized by the absence of the capacity for any designation (*upākhyā*), a cloud may nevertheless remain by the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings.

And just as a Vidyādhara, with the intention of [creating] a world, presides over the wind-circle, the wind, and trees with untimely flowers by the power of mantra, so too does he do so by the power of the nature of dependent origination.

In the same way, the wise and learned Bodhisattva, understanding the path of vision (darśanamārga) as it has just been described along with its causes, does not perceive any object of cognition (padārtha) superimposed by the conceptualization of a grasper based on the side of active involvement (pravṛttipakṣa), nor does he perceive any phenomena (sarvadharma) established by the conceptualization of a grasper based on the side of cessation (nivṛttipakṣa); nor does he perceive a teacher superimposed by the conceptualization of a grasper based on a substantially existent person (dravyasatpuruṣa), nor even a seer.

It is established as the conceptualization of a grasper based on a person who exists only nominally (*prajñaptisat*). This is because, through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the four aforementioned conceptualizations are abandoned. Therefore, for those who desire non-abiding nirvana within the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—the fixed order of dependent origination—this dwelling is the path of seeing accompanied by the causes as described; it is established for those followers of the Jina’s way who delight in qualities such as the ten powers. This is the intended meaning. (5–6)

If it is argued that this dwelling of the śrāvakas is identical to the path of the bodhisattvas, he says: "As many as," and so forth. Setting aside the dwelling in liberation of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, there are as many dwellings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas as are characterized by the paths of vision and so forth; these are peaceful because they function to abandon the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Because it acts as the basis for dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) during the state of tranquility through one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*), these [attainments] are associated with pleasure; yet among all of them, this dwelling is the foremost, and it is unsurpassed because it functions to abandon the additional cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) through the yoga of attaining qualities uncommon to the Sons of the Conquerors (*jinatanaya*). // 7 //

If it is asked, "Since [the bodhisattva] is distinguished above all others, why does he not go to nirvāṇa and so forth? he says: "Like space," and so on. Just as a bird dwells in space and does not fall—even though there is no obstruction to its flight in space—due to the power of its two wings produced by its own effort; and just as a fish dwells in the midst of water and does not die from a lack of breath, through the sovereign influence of its own karma.

Thus, there, by virtue of attaining skill in means (*upāyakauśala*), the Bodhisattva who has likewise reached the perfection of the power of meditative concentration (*dhyānabala-pāramitā*)—by bringing before him the path of vision which is like an illusion (*māyopama-darśanamārga*) and while abiding in emptiness (*śūnyatā-vihārī*)—does not yet attain final extinction (*nirvṛti*). The sense is that this is due to the power of the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) instilled by his previous vows (*pūrvapraṇidhāna*). // 8 //

Therefore, concluding that those who desire to realize all goals must cultivate this very dwelling, he says "He who," and so forth: He who desires preeminence among all sentient beings through his qualities—that is, the attainment of the *dharmakāya*—and who desires to touch the supreme *saṃbhogakāya*; he who would wish for the most wonderful Buddha-gnosis;

and he who wishes to bestow the supreme [benefit] by means of the *nirmāṇakāya*—in order to accomplish the welfare of self and others respectively—he should correctly cultivate this supreme dwelling, which is the excellent and ultimate gift of Dharma for the Bodhisattvas who act for the benefit of others. (9)
The twenty-seventh chapter, "The Essence," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*.
The twenty-eighth chapter, "The Chapter on Scattered Flowers.

Furthermore, what is this Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi) for the sake of which the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), accompanied by the causes as previously described, is intended? Thus, explaining the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Great Enlightenment, he says: "As many as... and so forth.

Whatever trainings have been elucidated by the Guide, who acts as the charioteer for the worlds, through the sequence beginning with the generation of the thought of awakening—may I train in those trainings within the Great Awakening, which consists of the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising because they are like an illusion due to the absence of exhaustion and non-arising; and may that distinguished knowledge become supreme and unsurpassed through the application of abandonment in its proper order.

Therefore, whoever among those learned in all the trainings desires to go to the further shore, they should correctly cultivate this perfection of wisdom—the training for Buddhahood whose nature is the path as it has been described; such is the meaning. // 1 //

Having concluded what arose incidentally, he now speaks to explain the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) which is the actual subject at hand, beginning with the words "the supreme," and so forth. Because it is the non-perversion resulting from the non-apprehension of all things, and because it comprises the wholesome factors already attained, it is the "supreme treasury. This single-moment [wisdom] included within the acceptance of the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) during the culminating clear realization (*mūrdhābhisamaya*)—manifested through the purity of the three spheres in giving and the other perfections, and produced from the thirty-six aspects—is the "supreme treasury of Dharma" due to the acquisition of a Dharma not previously possessed.

And therefore, because it produces the dharma that arises as the attainment of Buddhahood, it is the progenitor of the lineage (*gotra*) of the Buddhas; and because it brings to completion the ten stages beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*), it would be a treasury of bliss and happiness.

Thus, because they have demonstrated nirvāṇa in this gradual manner, they are "past"; because they will bring about Buddhahood, they are "future"; and because they perform the welfare of the world by existing in the ten directions in the present, they are the "Lords of the World," the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Since they possess the nature of having attained the ultimate limit of the fourfold conceptualization of subject and object, and since they have necessarily abandoned [these concepts] starting from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—which is connected to the "Summit Realization" (*mūrdhābhisamaya*) on the tenth stage—they have all arisen from that [path] in due order.

They will give birth [to it] and continue to give birth [to it]; yet this does not diminish, because even though it is realized by all Tathāgatas, it is the path of seeing the dharmadhātu by virtue of its nature as emptiness—this is the meaning. // 2 //

Therefore, explaining with an illustration how this is the cause for the perfection of all virtues through the abandonment of all fear, he says: "As many as... and so forth. Just as whatever flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, or forest giants there are in the world, they all emerge from the earth through a manifestation never before seen, appearing through the process of successive growth; yet the earth does not undergo exhaustion by the excessive weight of that which has been described, nor even due to the accumulation of trees and the like.

They do not increase because they lack exertion, nor do they disappear because they lack invisibility; for, due to the absence of all conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts, they are non-conceptual.

Likewise, however many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, Arhats, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and gods there may be, and whatever dharmas of happiness and well-being exist for the entire world—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—all of these are born from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), specifically from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) as it has been described, and from the Bodhisattva who cultivates it. Just so, because of the absence of all conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts (*kalpa-vikalpa*), this wisdom neither diminishes nor ever increases; "wisdom" here refers to the path of seeing in the correct awakening to the Dharma. (3–4)

Having thus explained the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), [the author notes that] the abandonment of opposing factors and so forth is easily understood once the foundational practice (*ādhārapratipatti*) has been established; therefore, he first speaks of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as the foundation, in order to explain it as the cause for the perfection of all virtues, preceded by examples, beginning with the words "As many as... and so forth. Just as there exist in the world beings who are inferior due to their connection with inferior qualities and so forth, those who are middling due to their connection with middling substances and so forth, and those who are superior due to their connection with the most excellent activities.

The Sugata has taught that all these [phenomena], by way of negating their permanence, eternity, and so forth, arise from ignorance on the level of conventional reality (saṃvṛti), because they have the causes of previous virtuous karma. Likewise, the causal complex of the "impelling" karma sets the machine of the five aggregates of grasping (pañcopādānaskandha) in motion for as long as the projected duration lasts; yet the machine does not consist of ignorance itself, nor does ignorance diminish, nor does it increase, because even conventionally there is no arising of a previously non-existent sentient being—this is the intended meaning.

Likewise, as many modes of knowledge (*jñānanaya*) as there are within the three vehicles—characterized by specific types of knowledge and, according to their sequence, being weak, middling, and superior—they serve as the doors and means for attaining progressively higher goals; all of these [roots] are conventionally produced from the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) by the bodhisattva who cultivates them throughout the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

In this way, the causal complex of impelling karma sets it in motion until the end of saṃsāra through mutual cooperation as a machine of cognition; yet, because it is like an illusion, the path of practicing the perfection of wisdom does not, in reality, increase or diminish. (5–6)

In what manner has he realized this so that he becomes a bearer of the aforementioned qualities? To this he says: "But here," and so forth. That Bodhisattva who, because dependent origination itself is like an illusion and thus lacks exhaustion, understands this perfection of wisdom—characterized by the attainment of the *avaskandha-samāpatti*—as the path of cultivation precisely through its inexhaustibility; he, like the sun released from masses of clouds, dispels darkness with its rays and shines forth of its own accord.
Having shaken off that veil of ignorance, the Blessed One, the Self-Existent One, becomes like a Tathāgata named Avakīrṇakusuma. // 7 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Scattered Flowers."
The twenty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on Following.

Having thus explained the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), [the author] says "by four," etc., in order to first state that which is to be abandoned therein—the two types of conceptualization regarding the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakavikalpa*), which are each fourfold. Meditation (*dhyāna*) is fourfold due to the distinction between the fulfillment of one's own and others' welfare, and likewise due to the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate.

By means of these four forms of one-pointedness of mind, he dwells by taking as his object the path of cultivation characterized by the nine successive meditative attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) in its progressive order; through the abandonment of the two types of conceptualization regarding the apprehended (*grāhyavikalpa*), he possesses great majesty due to the greatness of the realization attained. Furthermore, because he has abandoned the two types of conceptualization regarding the apprehended, he does not, through the application of attachment, make a storehouse (*ālaya*) nor a basis (*niśraya*) out of those states by way of grasping.

Furthermore, because they are the basis for the two accumulations and the cause [of the result], these four types of mental one-pointedness, which are the objects of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), will become supreme here. The sense is that, through the application of distinguished knowledge and abandonment, one dwells by means of these for the sake of attaining the excellent enlightenment—the supreme enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and others—because it is preeminent. (1)

Immediately following this, in order to indicate the two types of conceptualization regarding the subject (*grāhaka*) that are to be abandoned, he says "in meditation" (*dhyāne*), and so forth. A bodhisattva who is established here in the meditation just mentioned becomes a possessor of supreme wisdom through the attainment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) by means of abandoning the two types of conceptualization regarding the subject. This is because the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*)—since they have the nature of the meditations of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)—are four "material" concentrations (*rūpisamādhi*), and by the word "and" (*ca*), the single attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is also included.

Since all of these are cultivated through the union of wisdom and skillful means, they are the most excellent meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). Because these are correctly practiced again and again, they become beneficial in that they are conducive to the supreme awakening which has meditation as its intrinsic nature. Nevertheless, because there remains a remainder of what is to be done—due to the absence of effort in abandoning the obscurations to the stage of a Buddha—the Bodhisattva does not yet train for the total exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*). // 2 //

By means of the abandonment of the four types of conceptual construction, he explains that this is the cause of the perfection of all virtues, saying: "It is wonderful," and so forth. Because the cause is great, it is wonderful; because the fruit is great, it is marvelous. This conduct is the basis for the accumulation of virtues for Bodhisattvas—that is, by dwelling in the path of cultivating meditative concentration attained through the aforementioned fourfold types of dhyāna—even while there is the apprehension of that [state].

Because there is an absence of attachment therein, no sign exists. Furthermore, while established on that path of cultivation, if their own personal existence (*svātmabhāva*) is dissolved through the abandonment of the remaining obscurations, then—since rebirth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is in every way prohibited as will be explained later—they are born, out of dependence upon compassion, in whichever of the two realms, desire or form, they have desired, such as in a family of kṣatriyas or others, according to their intention. (3)

Explaining by means of an analogy for the sake of the uninterrupted concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), he says "just as" and so forth: Just as the humans of Jambudvīpa, because they have never before obtained it, do not attain the divine realms such as the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, nor do they reach Uttarakuru.

Because they travel by means of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth, and because they have grasped their objects there through vision and enjoyment, they might return again to perform the welfare of sentient beings who depend upon them; yet they would not create any obstruction there, for that place is the cause of infinite bliss previously experienced. Likewise, those very ones who possess qualities through the realization of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are the excellent Bodhisattvas, as they are superior to those mentioned before.

Abiding through meditation that takes non-existence as its object and through the recollection of wholesome qualities as the dominant condition, they apply themselves to the uninterrupted concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*) by way of the aspect of tranquility. Furthermore, because the word "desire" (*kāma*) here denotes what is desired—referring to the desire realm while excluding the formless realm—they remain in one of those realms out of compassion for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings. Yet, being unstained by the defects belonging to those realms, they remain untainted like lotuses in water.

Therefore, they are non-reliant because they do not rely on the dharma of apprehending giving and so forth, which is the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). In this context, the misconceptions that proliferate as a succession of objections from those who have not understood the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva—arising because [this state] is difficult to grasp—must be refuted. (4–5)

In that regard, if it is asked, "If they are indeed non-reliant (*aniśrita*), how can there be the attainment of objects of focus and so forth?", he says: "Elsewhere," and so on. Because they bring sentient beings to maturity through the teaching of the Dharma and other means, because they purify their own minds and thereby purify the Buddha-field, and because they strive to fulfill these perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity by abandoning their opposites, the great-souled Bodhisattvas are not reliant upon anything else.

What, then, is the purpose of this? Therefore, since the conditions such as the arising of the objective support (*ālambana*) are possible in two realms, the followers of the Jina do not seek their own rebirth above the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)—in the four locations designated as the Sphere of Infinite Space and so forth—in accordance with the Mahāyāna sūtras which describe the designation of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This is because, due to the cessation of all perceptions resulting from the arising of calm abiding (*śamatha*), there would be a loss of the supreme qualities of awakening, namely the perfections (*pāramitā*). // 6 //

If they are not greedy because of the coating of defects inherent in that [treasure], for what purpose do they remain there? Answering this by means of an illustration, he says "Just as," and so forth: Just as a certain man, upon finding a treasure consisting of jewels, does not conceive a mind of longing for it due to the absence of any personal need;

and because it is unknown to others, he takes that treasure alone and, at another time, enters his own house divided from his kinsmen—yet even so, he does not become greedy, because his activity is directed toward another purpose.

Through the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), by means of the four aforementioned meditations (*dhyāna*) which are conducive to concentration (*samādhi*), the wise Bodhisattvas attain peaceful liberations (*vimokṣa*) that bestow joy and bliss. Because they lack any attachment (*avagraha*) therein, they relinquish the meditative bliss characterized by their own self-interest—both in its conventional and ultimate aspects—and according to the sequence [of practice], they enter again into the aforementioned realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) by manifesting a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) through the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Therefore, because they remain out of compassion for the world, it is understood that they have no attachment to that [state]. // 7–8 //

If that is so, then how is it that there is no distraction due to entering the stage of non-concentration? To this [the author says], "If," and so forth. If a bodhisattva, even while remaining in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), dwells in a concentration that has one-pointedness of mind as its object, yet because he attends only to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he gives rise to a longing for the state of a *dhyāna*-attainer or for the state of a *pratyekabuddha*.

Because he is impartial toward the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), he is free from the objects of his own preferred interests; because he is agitated by the fault of apprehension (*upalambha*), he is unconcentrated (*asamāhita*); because his mind is excited, his mind has gone outside the Mahāyāna, and thus his mind is distracted (*kṣiptacitta*). Consequently, he has fallen away from the qualities of a Buddha, like a boatman whose net is torn apart and whose goods are lost. However, it is not merely by way of non-attainment or simple non-arising that he is unconcentrated; rather, the intention is that he is so through the power of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*). // 9 //

Explaining that very point, he says: "Furthermore," and so forth. Even if, through the cultivation of phenomena as being like an illusion, or for the sake of such purposes as gathering in sentient beings, one becomes intent upon the five strands of sensual pleasure—form and the rest—one is nevertheless free from a mind of longing for the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. However, regarding the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) which has emptiness and compassion as its core, you must understand that one is not constantly concentrated upon it because of the loss of that very desired object. A Bodhisattva would be a hero by virtue of having conquered all adversaries.

When it is said that misconceptions have been refuted through such a succession of logical consequences (*prasaṅga*), that is the "culminating clear realization" (*mūrdhābhisamaya*). And so it has been said:
"The sign of that is the firm establishment of the mind, characterized by increase;
and there are four kinds of antidotes for the fourfold conceptualization."

On each of the two paths known as "seeing" (*darśana*) and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), there is the uninterrupted concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*) along with its opposing factors; this is called the "culminating clear realization" (*mūrdhābhisamaya*). (Abhidharmasamuccaya 1.15–17) // 10 //

Having attained the *mūrdhābhisamaya* (culminating clear realization), one brings the objects realized both individually and collectively into their proper sequence and contemplates them for the sake of stabilization; thus, for the purpose of the *anupūrvābhisamaya* (sequential clear realization), he says "pare" and so forth. Supreme (*para*) beings are filled (*pūryante*) and overflow (*galanti*) with the latencies (*vāsanā*) of virtue and so on; because of those persons, all faults are removed, and being of purified mind, there arise the six perfections beginning with generosity, the six recollections beginning with the Buddha, and the fact that all phenomena have the nature of non-existence.

Thus, through the cultivation of the thirteen kinds of dharmas, those devoted to the supreme perfection of vigor proceed. Just as a water-carrier slave girl, by performing the tasks as instructed, becomes submissive through her lack of independence and lack of self-mastery, yet becomes compliant by being subject to the will of her master.

Likewise, because their conduct is dependent upon all sentient beings, steadfast Bodhisattvas attain mastery, since they cannot be disturbed in any way; thus has the progressive resolve been described. And so it is said: "The progressive [resolve] is threefold and tenfold" (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 1.17). // 11 //

For the sake of making those very [stages] well-practiced by one who has already cultivated the gradual realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*), there is the attainment of them in a single moment; thus, for the purpose of explaining the "awakening in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), he says "And not... and so forth, preceded by an illustration.

Just as a female servant does not give a reply to her master, because she speaks unpleasantly in a manner contrary to his wishes; even when reviled, struck with a rod or the like, or beaten with his hand, she remains entirely with a terrified mind, overwhelmed by humiliation, and filled with fear. The implication is that she thinks: "Lest my master strike me again for the very reason of my giving a reply."

Likewise, a bodhisattva who has set out for supreme enlightenment, through the fourfold manner of awakening—such as the single-moment complete awakening characterized by all dharmas being non-retributive and untainted—[effects this] within the *ālayavijñāna* by means of the mutual relationship of cause and fruit between the latencies (*vāsanā*) of all dharmas resting therein and the focal objects of any particular untainted dharma such as giving; thus, by virtue of depending on a single totality (*sāmagrī*), he achieves realization in a single moment due to the cause of its being distinguished by excellence.

Thus one should remain toward all beings in the world, having abandoned all obscurations, by becoming their servant through the practice of honoring them; for from this honoring of sentient beings comes the attainment of enlightenment as its fruit, and the fulfillment of the qualities that serve as its causes. Otherwise, just as a fire produced from grass and wood burns up that very same grass and wood when it blazes, so too do sentient beings, when provoked to anger, destroy the Dharma produced from them—such is the understanding.

Thus has been explained this "awakening in a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*). And so it has been said: "In the awakening in a single moment, there are four types according to their characteristics" (*Abhisamayālaṃkāra* 1.17). // 12–13 //

For one who has realized the awakening of a single moment (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodha*), there is the realization of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāyābhisambodha*) in the second moment; for that purpose, he says "having relinquished" (*avasṛjya*), and so forth. Just as a mother, while properly attending to her only son, remains unwearying in her disposition because she is free from deceit and the like, and thus attends upon him; in the same way, through the attainment of the activity of the four bodies—the Essential Body (*svābhāvikakāya*) and the others—by being oriented toward great compassion and so forth which take all beings as their object, he has relinquished his own personal happiness and is devoted day and night to the welfare of other sentient beings.

Because he is free from even the expectation of such benefit, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, remains present with a mind devoid of desire for recompense. Thus has been explained the perfect awakening to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). And so it is said:

"The essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*), the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*), and likewise the other, the emanation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*), along with the Dharma-body together with its activity—thus is it proclaimed as fourfold. (Abhisamayālaṃkāra 1.18)

Thus, this eightfold realization has been presented in its entirety as a summary for the instruction of ordinary people; however, the detailed exposition should be understood from the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-nibandhana* by those who desire to train. Since it is impossible to apply every aspect [of the meaning] even when there is a specific purpose regarding a particular distinction, nothing has been definitively included under the category of abbreviation elsewhere because it is stated in full.
Thus, that which is not intended to be expressed is merely reduced to the category of what is intended to be expressed; therefore, that [opinion] was not introduced and then refuted. // 14 //
The twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Following," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthāvyākhyā*.

Explaining what kind of practice must be performed to please the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the sake of attaining the Mother—whose nature is the eightfold realization (*aṣṭābhisamaya*)—through the arising of knowledge from hearing [the Dharma] and so forth, he says: "The bodhisattva who... and so on.

That bodhisattva who, with the intention of wandering for a long time in cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings, and likewise, being a practitioner of yoga through the yoga authorized by the Buddhas in the purification of the Buddha-fields according to the distinction between the support and the supported, does not produce even an atom of weariness toward non-attainment due to the power of cultivating phenomena as being like an illusion; [that one is the best].

Through the realization of the perfection of wisdom, he becomes endowed with the threefold perfection of vigor—consisting of acting for the benefit of beings and so forth—based on the objective support of sentient beings; thus, he is free from sloth and torpor and remains untiring. // 1 //

When the thought of weariness arises, what is the fault? To demonstrate this, he says "He [who thinks... and so forth. If one thinks that awakening is attained by Buddhas only after ten million eons (*kalpa*), then an ignorant bodhisattva, having formed a long-lasting notion regarding the awakening of a Tathāgata, will suffer for a long time due to the notion of suffering. Because of his attachment to objective apprehension (*upalambha*), he understands phenomena in such a way; and because he has thus fallen away from the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), he is deficient, and consequently, his nature becomes that of the quality of laziness (*kausīdya*).

If one asks, "How then is the thought of weariness not to be produced? he says: "From the very beginning," and so forth. From the initial generation of the mind for supreme enlightenment until one attains the unsurpassed, auspicious state of the Tathāgatas—by means of this method, because weariness is removed, the wise and learned person who has initiated vigor should be known [as such]. //3//

Thinking that there might be disturbances caused by Māra due to his correct engagement, he says, "And he," and so forth. If someone were to say, "Having split Sumeru, the king of mountains, you shall thus attain supreme enlightenment," and having heard this, because it is perceived as something impossible to accomplish, he should form a notion of weariness—realizing the magnitude of Sumeru to be eighty thousand *yojanas*—then the Son of the Victor would fall into laziness; and for that reason, the thought is that he would not attain enlightenment. (4)

If it is asked, "How then is that [insight] realized?", he says: "Now," and so forth. Now, even if a thought arises in him, because it is produced from a contrary latent impression (*vāsanā*), it is not the arising of correct knowledge; nevertheless, O wise one, the Bodhisattva should exert his vigor, thinking: "In a mere moment, I shall reduce even a tiny atom of Mount Sumeru to ashes and lead it to destruction. And for this reason, he will before long attain supreme enlightenment—that is to say, the state belonging to the Guides, the Blessed Ones. // 5 //

Even when effort is free from its opposites, the apprehension of a real entity is a fault; thus he says, "And that," and so forth. If, with the intention, "By means of miracles—namely, the miracle of teaching and the miracle of psychic power—and by the miracle of instruction, I shall accomplish the welfare of the world," one exerts oneself through body, mind, and speech, then because of the abundance of afflictions, one would fall into laziness. This is because, being devoid of the perception of others and remaining fixed in the perception of a self, [one acts for one's own sake].

Through the arising of the afflictions of attachment, the Son of the Victor would become far removed from the cultivation of selflessness which is like an illusion; for [the latter] has the characteristic of non-existence, whereas [the former] has the characteristic of existence, like space. And thus, he would not be one possessed of vigor—this is the meaning. (6)

How, then, is he endowed with that? He says: "In which," and so forth. In that state of being like an illusion (*māyopamatva*), there is nothing to be produced, nor is there a mind; since it serves as a mere indicator, there is neither speech nor even the notion of a sentient being (*sattvasaṃjñā*), due to the absence of apprehending any real entity.

In this regard, when one has turned back these conceptualizations (*saṃjñā*) and, being free from mental attention to existence and non-existence, dwells practicing the non-dual Dharma, then—due to the absence of all defects and imbalances—the Son of the Victor, endowed with the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*), aspires for the supreme enlightenment that is auspicious because it is free from all discordance and is unfallen due to its being non-abiding nirvāṇa; so it was declared by the Lord of the World, the Perfected One. Thus, by one who has set out in the search for a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and so forth, patience (*kṣānti*) must be practiced, otherwise the intended goal will not be accomplished. // 7 //

Speaking of the patience that endures harm from others (*parāpakāramarṣaṇakṣānti*) together with the patience of reflecting on the Dharma (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), he says "a person," and so forth. Having heard ill-spoken words from another—such as frivolous chatter (*sambhinnapralāpa*) arising from the afflictions—one generates satisfaction through the cultivation of patience, because it serves as a cause for acquiring merit and because one understands it as being like a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Because his face is serene, he is "fair-faced" (*sumukha*). Since that wise Bodhisattva [is thus], he reflects upon the subsequent speech: "Who speaks? Who hears? From where has it arisen? To whom does it belong? By what means is it perceived? However, because all phenomena (*dharma*) are like an illusion, through such investigation as "there is no speaker at all," that wise one is endowed with patience (*kṣānti*). This is the meaning of the verse: that he possesses the supreme perfection (*pāramitā*) whose nature is to endure the harm inflicted by others, accompanied by the profound contemplation of phenomena. // 8 //

To the question, "What is the merit in such patience? he says: "The bodhisattva who... and so forth. That bodhisattva who, through practice, endures the two types of patience just described—endowed respectively with compassion and wisdom, and thus possessed of virtuous qualities—and another person who were to give a great trichiliocosm world-system filled with jewels to the Buddhas, the World-Knowers, the Śrāvakas, and the Pratyekabuddhas: the merit of the former bodhisattva is [greater].

Because it produces a result that is inferior and immediate when compared [to the former], its merit is merely a fraction; since that [fraction] is its cause, it would not constitute a continuous stream of giving in this world. // 9 //

If it is asked, "Whence is this so?", he says: "Patience," and so forth. For one who abides in practice within the two kinds of patience, there is the acquisition of a pleasing physical form; and because that physical form is completely pure, it is adorned with the thirty-two marks. Because it is endowed with the eighty secondary signs, its radiance from the thirty-two marks is infinite and boundless.

And he observes that by means of his body being beyond satiety, he establishes sentient beings in faith regarding the results of karma and the ultimate Dharma. Furthermore, the wise one, practicing patience, becomes beloved throughout the entire world because he is free from enmity toward all. Since all of this is the fruit of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) and does not arise from the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), the intended meaning is that the position established in the previously cited verse alone is correct. // 10 //

Now, speaking of the patience that endures suffering together with the patience of reflecting on the Dharma, he says: "He... and so forth. If someone, out of great affection for their teacher, were to take a casket of sandalwood and scatter it over a Bodhisattva such as Devadatta, while another person were to throw a mass of fire upon his head, even then, by the power of cultivating the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one should maintain an equal mind toward both and generate the cause for awakening (*bodhinimitta*). // 11 //

Thus, having explained how patience should be cultivated as previously described, and that one must perform the dedication within that [patience], he says "In this way," and so forth, indicating the result with even greater emphasis:

When a wise and learned Bodhisattva, having become patient according to the sequence just mentioned, dedicates the arising of the mind associated with patience toward supreme enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, then he completely surpasses all the patiences whatsoever belonging to Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and the realm of sentient beings such as Bodhisattvas, throughout the entire world.

One who practices patience as it has been described is a hero, insofar as he cannot be overcome by others due to his superior dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and has thus conquered his adversaries. // 12 //

But how can forbearance (*kṣamaṇa*, *marṣaṇa*) toward the harm inflicted by others be practiced even when there is objective perception? To this he says: "Forbearance," and so forth. One who practices patience should further generate the following thought: "In the hells, among animals, and in the world of Yama, many sufferings have been experienced—sufferings that were unwanted because they resulted from the failure to achieve desired objects due to the cause of sensual pleasures. Why, then, do I not now practice patience for the sake of attaining such excellent dharmas as spiritual friends, which are the primary cause for enlightenment?"

The meaning is this: it is not because the word "what" implies a censure; rather, through the power of wisdom, one should endure the harm inflicted by others and so forth, thinking, "I shall simply act in this way. // 13 //

Explaining that very point, he says "in the case of a gash" (*kaśe*) and so forth: when there is a gashing from being struck with a cane or similar object; a flogging with a staff from the confiscation of gold and other property; a killing by a weapon from blows with a sword or the like; a binding from the imposition of chains and the like; and a beating from the infliction of pain on the hands and so forth.

"By removing the head, ears, feet, and so forth, there is their severance"—thinking in this way, "I am able to endure whatever sufferings of such a kind exist in the world for the sake of attaining the distinguished Dharma," when a bodhisattva performs such analytical reflection, then he should abide in the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), which has the aforementioned intrinsic nature, just like Sadāprarudita. // 14 //
The thirtieth chapter, titled "Sadāprarudita," in the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthāvyākhyā*.
The thirty-first chapter, "Dharmodgata.

Having thus described the search [for the Dharma], it is said—beginning with the words "In morality"—that spiritual friends should first provide instruction in morality (*śīla*), because it is the foundation of all virtues. Through the threefold morality consisting of restraint (*saṃvara*) and so forth, those who have risen up by undertaking [the precepts] with the aspiration for *nirvāṇa* and who desire peace through the adoption of restraint, they follow [the path] by accomplishing through practice as many acts of restraint as there are due to the activity of restraint.

And when they dedicate those [roots of virtue] for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings by directing them toward unsurpassed enlightenment, then, because they belong to the domain of the Ten-Powered Ones and because they are free from all transgressions, they abide in unbroken morality; such is the meaning of the verse to be applied. // 1 //

Clarifying this very point by means of a negative corollary (*vyatireka*), he says: "And if," and so forth. If one generates a longing for the enlightenment of the *pratyekabuddhas* and the *arhats* because of having undertaken vows and performed dedications [for their sake], then, due to being devoid of the practice of the Mahāyāna, one would be immoral (*duḥśīla*) and, by abandoning the vows thus undertaken, would become a transgressor in the eyes of the wise Tathāgatas. However, if one dedicates the morality undertaken for the sake of supreme, auspicious enlightenment (*bodhi*), [one is not so].

Thus established in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), because he does not abandon the goal he has grasped, he may even be joined with the qualities of sensual pleasure provided they do not conflict with his ethical discipline. // 2 //

If it is asked why instruction regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*) comes first, he says: "That which is the Dharma," and so forth. Because the arrival (*āgama*) of Bodhisattvas—the attainment of the perfection of their own welfare through the realization of the Dharma that fulfills both [self and other], and the perfection of the welfare of others through the acquisition of virtuous qualities—is due to the purpose of ethical discipline, which consists in protecting oneself from misfortune while being endowed with the qualities of the Dharma.

The Leader has revealed that for those Bodhisattvas who act for the benefit of others, any decline from the qualities of the awakening to the Dharma is connected with immorality; therefore, the sense is that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is the very first instruction. // 3 //

To the question of "By how much is one established in ethical discipline (*śīla*)?", he says "If," and so forth. If a bodhisattva, even while enjoying the five objects of sensual pleasure well-known in the world, maintains refuge in the Three Jewels until he reaches the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), thinking, "I shall become a Buddha who acts for the welfare of the world," and if omniscience remains present in his mind—by this much alone, through the undertaking of the vow of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta-saṃvara*), the wise one should be known as established in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). This is because, apart from this, the Mahāyāna sūtras provide extensive and preeminent instruction on the ethical discipline of the vow of awakening and so forth. (4)

To state briefly, however, that one is indeed of immoral conduct due to the absence of mental attention toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), he says "If," and so forth. If, while practicing for ten million eons through the ten wholesome paths of action such as abstaining from taking life, one generates a longing for the state of a Pratyekabuddha or an Arhat by dedicating one's morality (*śīla*) toward those ends, then—due to the persistence of former immorality—one would be of broken morality and thus likewise of immoral conduct.

Because, by generating the thought of enlightenment, one has invited [beings] to Buddhahood, to turn back from that is more serious than a root downfall or a *pārājika* offense due to deceiving sentient beings; this generation of the thought [is more serious] when it is accompanied by a longing for the state of a Śrāvaka and so forth. // 5 //

Even when right conduct has been authorized, [the author] says "protecting," and so forth, to explain how one should abide in it: while protecting the aforementioned ethical discipline—having first undertaken its formal adoption and having dedicated it toward supreme enlightenment—one does not, on account of that very discipline, disparage or hold others in contempt.

Nor does he exalt himself through the conceit of [superior] morality and observances (*śīlavratābhimāna*). Therefore, having abandoned the notion of a self as something to be grasped and likewise the notion of other beings as something to be rejected, he is then said to be "established in the perfection of morality (*śīlapāramitā*) as described. The meaning is that a bodhisattva should conduct himself in this very manner. // 6 //

Otherwise, however, there is indeed a fault; thus he says "yadi" and so forth. If a Bodhisattva, while practicing, because of his adherence to the morality of the Victors as previously described, establishes on the path that "these are virtuous" and "those are immoral" by way of what is to be rejected and what is to be adopted—then, since he has engaged in the perception of diversity among sentient beings, it is impossible to protect them in every respect through the apprehension of real entities (*vastūpalambha*). Consequently, just as before, others would be immoral, and likewise even one who is "leaky" in morality (*chidraśīla*) would for that very reason not be one of pure morality (*pariśuddhaśīla*). And thus, the sense is that when there is apprehension of real entities, one is not fit for [the practice]. // 7 //

And he says, "For one who courses in non-apprehension, there is no offense," beginning with the words "for whom not" and so forth. For one who, by the power of the illusory nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), has neither the notion of a self nor the notion of a sentient being, there is no lack of restraint (*asaṃvara*) because, due to the absence of the distinction between self and other, they are free from attachment and aversion; thus, when there is an aversion to grasping at signs, there is an absence of practicing prohibited things. And likewise, for such a person, there is no [clinging to] restraint (*saṃvara*), because that would entail the fault of adhering to mere rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), nor is there any obstruction to non-restraint, because there is no arising of unwholesome states.
Thus, this [discipline] has been revealed by the Leader through the restraint of ethical conduct (*śīlasaṃvara*), because it proceeds without error. // 8 //

Thus, he says "He who indeed... and so forth, to explain how one endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*) engages in giving: He who is thus endowed with the ethical discipline just mentioned—both conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*) and in its ultimate sense (*paramārthena*)—is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Precisely because of this, due to the absence of grasping (*avagraha*), he becomes indifferent toward all things, whether pleasant or unpleasant. Furthermore, by relinquishing his head and other limbs, he possesses an undaunted mind (*alīnacitta*) because there is no shrinking back when an object is being surrendered; by renouncing even existing wealth, he is a giver of everything (*sarvasvatyāgin*); and because of his constant lack of expectation regarding the fruits of giving, he remains undaunted. // 9 //

If it is asked, "How can he be one who renounces everything since there is no renunciation of external objects? he says: "Having known," and so forth. For when, by acting preceded by wisdom, one has understood that the nature of phenomena is insubstantial because their arising is dependent on causes at the level of conventional truth, and that they are selfless because they lack intrinsic nature at the level of ultimate truth—and yet, when giving away even one's own flesh and so forth, one’s mind does not shrink back—how much less would one fail to give away an external object? Thus, such a thing is impossible; he would never harbor stinginess regarding external objects. (10)

To the question, "For what purpose does one engage in giving through the yoga of selflessness? he says: "If I," and so forth. If there were a notion of "I" regarding the self and a sense of "mine"—characterized by attachment and non-renunciation—regarding that which belongs to the self, then the thought of renunciation would never arise for the deluded, who are shrouded by the darkness of objective apprehension (*upalambha*). And thus, due to their stinginess, they are reborn in the realms of hungry ghosts (*preta*); or if they somehow are reborn among humans, they become afflicted by poverty.
Therefore, engagement in giving is established precisely according to the principle stated above. (11)

If it is asked, "For what purpose is there such conviction in giving? he says: "At that time," and so forth. When he sees these poor beings, then the Bodhisattva, through the perfection of compassion, being one who has conviction in the aforementioned giving, becomes one who always practices relinquishment by abandoning all his possessions along with their fruits, because it is endowed with valid means of knowledge such as scripture. Therefore, having given away the four continents adorned with the seven jewels—which, due to the total absence of obstruction therein, are equal to [the state of] exhaustion—by way of the purification of the three spheres (*trimandala-pariśuddhi*).
Then he would attain joy, just as one who has obtained and reached the continents previously described—this is the meaning. // 12 //

And as it has been said—that giving should be dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of its inexhaustibility—it says "giving," and so forth. Having given a gift according to the sequence just described, the wise and learned Bodhisattva, having taken into account all sentient beings who exist within the three realms of existence, dedicates that vehicle toward supreme enlightenment with the intention: "May this gift given be for the benefit of all of them. For the sake of the world alone, because both enlightenment and sentient beings are inexhaustible, the gift shall be inexhaustible; such is the meaning. // 13 //

In that regard, demonstrating the fruit of non-attachment toward those [objects], he says "And not... and so forth. Because the gift, the giver, and the recipient are not perceived, one does not grasp at things as real entities; and having given a gift with a mind intent on successive benefit for others, one never at any time expects the ripening of its fruit out of a desire for its result.

Thus, having renounced all his own possessions along with their fruits, he becomes a wise man who has abandoned everything; and by abandoning even a small amount through the power of skillful means (*upāyakauśala*), he obtains a vast and immeasurable maturation (*vipāka*), because it is impossible to delimit it either by number or by measure—this is the remainder of the sense. // 14 //
