And for the sake of subduing stinginess, one should practice the dedication preceded by rejoicing, as if speaking of the perfection of generosity; thus he says "as many as," and so forth: however many sentient beings there are who exist in the entirety of the three realms—characterized by desire, form, and formlessness—because they are contained within the whole extent of the element of space.

And suppose all of them were to give gifts to the Buddhas, the World-Knowers, the Arhats, and the Pratyekabuddhas for infinite eons; likewise, if they desire the qualities of the Śrāvakas—and by implication, the qualities of the Buddhas and so forth—because their activity proceeds by way of apprehending real entities, the sense is that they remain in the state of conceptual construction.

Furthermore, another wise Bodhisattva who is skilled in the correct means, having rejoiced in those bases of meritorious action, should dedicate them toward supreme enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings; in this way, by suppressing stinginess, he shall surpass the entire world. (15–16)

One should dedicate the aforementioned [merit] as previously described. To illustrate this, he says: "Like glass," and so forth. Just as a single great *vaiḍūrya* jewel would surpass all the vast heaps of glass and ordinary gems by virtue of its superior value and radiance, even so the Bodhisattva who performs dedication according to the sequence just explained—preceded by sympathetic joy—surpasses the entire mass of extensive giving throughout the aforementioned world. (17)

Having explained the two perfections in detail, he says "If," and so forth, while giving instruction on the remaining perfections: when a bodhisattva, shining brightly through the preservation of the remaining perfections, performs the purification (or protection) of those very [perfections] as a gift related to the world, yet does not do so with the apprehension of a self or a sentient being therein.

And because of the realization that actions are devoid of intrinsic reality, one's attachment to things does not increase; rather, through the wholesome [factors], one becomes of great majesty, like the moon in the bright fortnight with its circles of radiance free from clouds. Thus, by means of instruction in the remaining perfections, the instruction on all goals—just as was done for the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata—should be carried out by a spiritual friend. // 18 //

Thus, having received the formal authorization, and through the sequence beginning with the generation of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), one attains the stages (*bhūmi*) such as the Joyous (*pramuditā*). To indicate that the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity (*dāna*) are primarily active at this point, he says: "Generosity," and so forth.

In that regard, primarily abiding on the Bodhisattva stage of *Pramuditā* (The Joyous), by abandoning stinginess through generosity, the Bodhisattva completely cuts off his own and all sentient beings' rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pretagati*) as well as their stinginess; likewise, he removes poverty and all afflictions (*kleśa*) such as suffering associated with it from the realms of gods and so forth. Furthermore, he obtains infinite, vast, and extensive enjoyments (*bhoga*) of various kinds.

While practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, one should bring beings to maturity by establishing them in the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and so forth through the practice of giving. Likewise, abiding in the *vimalā* stage, because of the departure from all immorality through the aforementioned ethical discipline (*śīla*), one avoids the various animal births and the eight well-known unfavorable conditions (*akṣaṇa*). Furthermore, one constantly attains the favorable conditions such as human birth, which accomplish distinguished goals.

In the *Prabhākarī* stage, due to the departure of all ill-will (*vyāpāda*), one attains form through patience, because it is adorned with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth; it is supreme because of its extreme vastness; it is noble because it resembles refined gold; it has a golden complexion because it is pleasing to the mind; and it is beloved because of its enchanting body, such that it becomes something the world cannot look upon enough. In the *Arciṣmatī* stage, due to the departure of all laziness (*kauśīdya*), one does not fall away from pure qualities (*śuklaguṇa*) by means of vigor, and one's knowledge is infinite because its objects are infinite.

Because it consists of the accumulation of the supreme wealth of Buddhahood, one attains the treasury and storehouse of the Victors. In the stage of "Very Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*), through the abandonment of all distractions by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one relinquishes the objects of sensual desire—which are the causes of distraction—by completely renouncing them as faults, stains, and things to be censured. Because its nature consists of the realization of the distinguished truths and the five supernormal knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), one possesses knowledge and supernormal powers in their proper sequence. Furthermore, through the production of samādhis such as the *Śūraṅgama*, one brings them forth.

And in the stage of Presence (*ābhimukhī*), through the departure of all faults and ignorance, one thoroughly understands the fundamental nature of phenomena as being like an illusion and so forth; by means of wisdom, one correctly transcends the three realms, the miserable states, and the bonds of perversion. Then, having first set in motion the precious wheel of Dharma with a cloud of emanations, one subsequently teaches the Dharma—comprised within the three vehicles—in succession to the Tathāgatas, for the sake of turning back the suffering of perversion in the world of sentient beings.

While fulfilling the practices such as generosity (*dāna*) through the power of skillful means (*upāya*) on the stage of *Dūraṅgamā*, that bodhisattva, by the force of his vows (*praṇidhāna*) on the stage of *Acalā*, attains the purification of the supporting Buddha-field by producing ground-sites made of gold and other precious materials, and the purification of the supported Buddha-field beings by ensuring the absence of hunger and other such afflictions. All these qualities of giving and the rest are perfected in their nature as perfections (*pāramitā*).

Likewise, on the stage of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), by means of the power of his strength, he sustains the lineage of the Buddhas (*buddhavaṃśa*) because he establishes the realm of sentient beings in Buddha-fields. Similarly, on the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), through the power of his gnosis, he sustains the lineage of the Dharma (*dharmavaṃśa*) due to the continuity of his teaching of the Dharma, and he sustains the lineage of the Saṅgha (*saṃghavaṃśa*) by producing an uninterrupted succession of Bodhisattvas.

Thus, in due order, on the eleventh stage, the Samantaprabhā, which is the Buddha-stage, one grasps all phenomena through the realization of the Dharma without error, by virtue of having abandoned all obscurations along with their latent tendencies. (1–5)

Having thus explained the Mother in detail, he speaks as follows—beginning with "The supreme physician of the world"—as a means of ensuring her long endurance. Just as one who, through excellence, removes fevers and other diseases from the world after having thoroughly mastered the definitions and the defined is called by a name corresponding to its meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), so too is she called the "Supreme Physician" because she possesses qualities such as the generation of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*). Furthermore, because she is a collection of various jewels (*ratna*) consisting of the accumulation of such qualities, she is the "Accumulation of Jewel-Qualities" (*ratnaguṇasañcaya*). Because she is set forth in metrical verse, she has the nature of a *gāthā*.

It should be understood that he entrusted [the teaching] to Ārya Ānanda and others with these words: "Just as all sentient beings have attained the path through this sequence of instruction on cultivation by means of the discourse on the non-duality of beings, so too must you act. This is because it is stated thus at the conclusion of the *Śatasāhasrikā Bhagavatī*.

In this regard, the sequence for the instruction on cultivation that produces firm conviction is as follows: first, having established oneself in an auspicious place, one should visualize the Teacher, the Blessed One, the Sovereign of the Śākyas, seated upon a lion throne and joined with the mudrā of the Wheel of Dharma; having performed worship according to the rules, and having visualized him surrounded by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, one should prostrate.

Then, having assumed the vajra-paryaṅka posture and established the body straight, remaining in the yoga of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), placing the tongue against the palate, and fixing the gaze on the tip of the nose, one should first take as an object of focus (*ālambana*) the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions. Having received instruction from them, one should grasp by name with the *mūlacitta* (root-mind) the method of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā-naya*) which illuminates the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*). Then, one should examine its various divisions—such as the distinctions between chapters (*parivarta*) and so forth—with the *anucara-citta* (following-mind).

Then, one should investigate with the mind by means of four aspects: through *gaṇanā* (counting), because one grasps the number by distinguishing the eight stages of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) and determines the specific nature of each realization; through *tulanā* (comparison), because there is an absence of superimposition and denial; through *mīmāṃsā* (investigation), because it is established by the valid cognitions of direct perception and inference; and through *pratyavekṣaṇā* (examination), which is the investigation of the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā* in these four ways. As for the syllables, however, one should investigate them by means of two aspects—individually and collectively—in the order of being "meaningless" and "possessing true meaning."

Then, having determined with a mind of ascertainment that "this very object as it was investigated is the truth, and anything else is delusion," one casts the very object as it was investigated—which is the basis for the names of signs—into the root-mind (*mūlacitta*) which apprehends those signs and names; and with a mind accompanied by the aspiration for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, one teaches [the following]: through the eye of wisdom, because all phenomena are not seen due to the light of correct knowledge in their likeness to an illusion, one does not conceptualize them, since they are empty, being devoid of the nature of cause and effect.

Then, because of the deficiency of both specific and general causes, they are signless (*animitta*); because of the non-perception of any object to be sought, they are wishless (*apraṇihita*). Thus, through the samādhi that is the gate of liberation which is naturally luminous, and by means of the sequential stages of the arousal of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), one should practice with a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) in order to uplift the realm of sentient beings who are bound within the prison of *saṃsāra* by the fetters of perversion due to their lack of thorough knowledge of the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*).

In that concentration, there are six faults: laziness, loss of the object of focus, lethargy and excitement, as well as [the lack of] application and [excessive] application; when these arise at their respective times, one should cultivate the eight formative forces of abandonment as appropriate antidotes. For instance, through faith characterized by deep conviction in the qualities of concentration, the practitioner generates desire; from the power of that desire, one initiates vigor.

Then, by the power of vigor (*vīrya*), one attains physical and mental pliancy (*prasrabdhi*). For one whose body and mind are pliant, laziness (*kauśīdya*) is turned away. Therefore, the four [faculties] beginning with faith serve for the abandonment of laziness. Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the antidote to the loss of the object of focus, because through it one remains correctly established upon the object.

Clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) is the antidote to lethargy (*laya*) and excitement (*auddhatya*); through it, by attending to the qualities of the Buddha and others which are objects of joy, lethargy is abandoned, and by attending to objects such as impermanence which induce a sense of urgency (*saṃvega*), excitement is abandoned.

At the time of pacifying laxity and excitement, the fault of non-application (*anābhoga*) arises; as its antidote, volition (*cetanā*) should be practiced. Once laxity and excitement have been pacified, when the mind proceeds toward the object of observation (*ālambana*) unwaveringly and flows without deliberate effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), then application (*ābhoga*) becomes a fault because it distracts the mind. Therefore, as its antidote, equanimity (*upekṣā*) should be cultivated. Having thus analyzed the sequence, one should first emerge from meditative absorption and, through the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) of being in the form of the compiler Śrīvajradhara, [proceed].

Having summoned the bodhisattvas and others, one should give the gift of Dharma by teaching the Perfection of Wisdom; then, through the yoga of non-attachment, one should dedicate all of that for the sake of all sentient beings toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—thus [is the practice] for the four classes of beings during the intermediate periods. // 6 //
In the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vyākhyā*, this is the thirty-second chapter, titled "Entrustment."

This [treatise], which was not understood by any former masters such as Purāṇa and others because they lacked the methods of yoga, and which has been brought forth by the Lord who has caused all the darkness of delusion to set—having explained it with words joined by sound reasoning, whatever merit I have gained thereby, may people quickly attain this [work] which abounds in a collection of the jewels of virtue.
This is the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*; [this work] is a clarification of its summarized meaning.
This *Śubhodayā*, an exposition of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, is completed.
It should be known that this work, composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter, consists of two thousand verses with an additional hundred counted as a total.
This is the work of the venerable teacher Haribhadra.
